title: Where a Model's 'Default' Answer Comes From
description: What it means when an AI tool fills in a gap you didn't specify — and why that fill-in is a statistic about training text, not a neutral or correct baseline.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that a model's default output is the statistically most common completion in its training distribution, not a neutral baseline
Predict which cases a model's default will underserve, given what's known about training-data skew
Recognize when a confident-sounding default is worth checking rather than trusting

contentSections.title: A default is a guess, not a finding

contentSections.body: You ask an AI tool to "generate 10 sample user profiles to test a signup form." It hands back names like Jason, Emily, Michael, Sarah — all in their late twenties or thirties, all able-bodied, all with a first-and-last-name-fits-one-line kind of name, none with a household of more than two adults. You didn't ask for any of that. You asked for ten users. This is what showed up when the request left room to guess.

An AI model generates text one likely-next-piece at a time, scored against everything it was trained on. When your prompt fully specifies what you want, there's nothing left to guess. When it doesn't — "ten users," "a nurse," "a shipping form" — the model fills the gap with whatever pattern showed up most often, in that shape, across its training text.

That's the whole mechanism behind a "default." It isn't the model's opinion about what a typical user looks like, and it isn't a deliberate choice on anyone's part. It's a statistic about what was overrepresented in the text the model learned from, surfaced without anyone asking it to be surfaced. Calling it "the default" makes it sound considered. It's closer to: whatever was already most common wins by default, because nothing pushed back on it.

contentSections.scenario: You ask an AI coding assistant to generate a shipping-address form for an online store. It returns a required "State" field (a dropdown of US states) and no "Country" field at all.
contentSections.question: What does that default most likely reflect?

options.label: The assistant decided this store only ships within the US
US-shaped address forms were the overwhelmingly common pattern among training examples that looked like this request

feedback.decision: Nothing in the prompt said US-only, so there was no decision to make about your store's shipping policy — the assistant wasn't told, and it didn't ask. What filled the gap wasn't a judgment call about your business.
feedback.skew: Right. Publicly available code, tutorials, and Stack Overflow answers for "address form" skew heavily US-shaped — English-language, US-hosted, US-market. The model reproduced the majority pattern from that text, not a decision about your store.

contentSections.concept: A default is the single most statistically common completion for an underspecified prompt, drawn from the model's whole training distribution — not a considered choice, and not evidence that the common case is the right case for your situation.

contentSections.body: A default isn't neutral — it's the most common pattern in the training data, surfaced because nothing in your prompt overrode it.

contentSections.title: What a default predicts about the edges

contentSections.body: A tax-prep chatbot answers a US filing question fluently, citing the right form numbers and deadlines. Ask it the equivalent question about a country with far less English-language tax documentation online, and the tone doesn't change — it still sounds just as confident. The accuracy does.

contentSections.scenario: You ask an AI code assistant, with no other detail, to write a `formatCurrency()` helper function.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of the time does a mainstream AI coding assistant default to USD formatting (a `$` sign, US thousands separators) rather than asking which currency you meant?
contentSections.explanation: Very high — in the large majority of cases, tools trained mostly on English-language, US-published code default straight to USD with no clarifying question. It's not that the model "prefers" dollars; it's that far more of the currency-formatting code it learned from was written for a USD context than for any other single currency, so USD is what a genuinely underspecified request resolves to.

contentSections.body: That's the specific, testable prediction worth carrying forward: **the model will be most accurate and most confidently correct on whatever showed up most often in training — and it will get vaguer, more generic, or flatly wrong on whatever showed up rarely, without its tone changing to signal the difference.** Confidence is the one signal most people actually use to decide whether to trust an answer, and it's exactly the signal that doesn't drop when the underlying data thins out. A model doesn't get quieter when it's guessing from three examples instead of three million. It reads the same either way.
A model's confidence doesn't drop on underrepresented cases — its accuracy does. That gap is exactly where you need to stop trusting the tone and start checking the content.

title: Whose Voices Are Overrepresented and Underrepresented in Training Data
description: Training text isn't a random sample of humanity — it's a sample of who had the time, access, and reason to publish in a form the model could scrape.

learningObjectives.text: Identify what kind of person's writing ends up overrepresented in web-scraped training text, and why
Classify a given topic or population as likely over- or underrepresented, and justify the classification

contentSections.title: Training text is a sample of who got to publish

contentSections.body: Wikipedia is one of the largest sources in most large models' training text. Editor surveys have repeatedly found that Wikipedia's editor base skews heavily male, disproportionately from North America and Western Europe, and disproportionately people with the free time to volunteer thousands of unpaid hours writing encyclopedia entries. That's not a flaw in Wikipedia — it's an extraordinary volunteer project. It's a fact about whose framing, whose notability judgments, and whose gaps ended up baked into a huge share of what a model reads as "general knowledge."

Web-scraped training text isn't a random sample of human experience. It's a sample of **who had internet access, time, reason, and confidence to publish text that was later crawled and kept** — filtered again by which languages and platforms crawlers prioritized. That stacks several real-world inequalities on top of each other before a single token is trained on:

- **Language.** English-language text dominates most large training sets, not because English speakers think more, but because more of the crawled, high-quality web happens to be in English.
- **Access and time.** Publishing takes reliable internet, often unpaid time, and platforms that don't require payment to post. That systematically favors people who aren't working multiple jobs, aren't managing a disability that makes typing costly, and live somewhere with stable connectivity.
- **Platform culture.** Reddit, GitHub, Stack Overflow, and similar heavily-scraped sites each have their own skewed user bases — GitHub's public repositories, for instance, are disproportionately written by professional developers in a handful of countries, not a cross-section of everyone who writes code.
- **What gets kept.** Even within "things people wrote," crawlers and cleaning pipelines favor well-formatted, high-traffic, frequently-linked text — which correlates with existing institutional reach more than with quality or truth.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding which of these are plausibly overrepresented versus underrepresented in a typical large model's training text, relative to their actual share of the world's population or activity.
contentSections.question: Select every group or topic you'd expect to be OVERrepresented relative to its real-world share.

items.label: English-speaking software developers publishing on GitHub and Stack Overflow
US and UK news and opinion writing
The demographic that dominates Wikipedia's volunteer editor base
Regional and minority languages with small numbers of fluent speakers
Knowledge traditionally passed on orally rather than in published text
Written perspectives from regions with historically low, expensive, or unreliable internet access

explanation.en-tech-writers: Overrepresented — English-language developer content on heavily-crawled platforms is a huge, disproportionate share of code-adjacent training text relative to how many of the world's developers actually write in English day to day.
explanation.us-news: Overrepresented — US and UK outlets are prolific, well-linked, and heavily crawled, which skews "general knowledge" toward their framing of events even for stories with a much wider global relevance.
explanation.wiki-editors: Overrepresented — the specific demographic that volunteers thousands of hours to Wikipedia is a narrow slice of humanity, and its notability judgments and gaps come along with everything it wrote.
explanation.regional-langs: Underrepresented — thin text in a minority language means thin, low-quality, or absent knowledge in that language, no matter how many people speak it day to day.
explanation.oral-cultures: Underrepresented — a model can only learn from what got written down and crawled. Knowledge that lives primarily in speech, practice, or apprenticeship largely isn't there at all, regardless of how central it is to the people who hold it.
explanation.low-connectivity: Underrepresented — publishing requires access in the first place. A region with historically expensive or unreliable internet produces less crawlable text per person, independent of how much is happening there worth writing about.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern isn't random and it isn't about which topics matter more — it's about who had the access, time, platform, and confidence to publish in a form a crawler would later keep. Every one of those filters correlates with existing advantage, which is why training-data skew tends to reproduce existing inequality rather than average it out.

contentSections.body: Overrepresentation in training text tracks who had access to publish, not who has something worth saying — and every filter along the way (language, platform, connectivity, free time) tends to favor the same people who already had more of everything else.

contentSections.title: What thin data does to the output

contentSections.body:
Underrepresentation doesn't just mean "less accurate." It changes shape depending on how thin the data gets:

**Moderately thin data** produces answers that are generic and lowest-common-denominator — technically not wrong, but stripped of the specific detail that would make them actually useful to someone in that situation. Ask about disability benefits in a mid-sized country with modest English documentation, and you'll often get a fluent-sounding answer that quietly blends rules from two or three different countries' systems.

**Very thin data** produces confident fabrication — the model pattern-matches to the closest well-documented case and fills in specifics that sound plausible but are invented, because there wasn't enough real signal to draw from and nothing in its training taught it to say "I don't actually know this one." (You'll go deeper on fabrication specifically in a later module — the mechanism is a close cousin of what's happening here.)

Both failure modes share the same tell: **the model's tone gives you no warning.** It doesn't hedge more on the thin-data answer. That's exactly why noticing the topic is thin has to be your job, not something the output will flag for you.

contentSections.scenario: A user asks an AI assistant to explain the sick-leave rules for a small country with limited English-language documentation online. The answer is fluent, specific, and cites concrete numbers — but two of the numbers turn out to be from a neighboring country's system, and one appears to be invented outright.
contentSections.question: What's actually going on here?

options.label: The model is deliberately being vague to avoid legal liability
Thin training data on this specific country pushed the model toward pattern-matching from better-documented neighbors and filling remaining gaps with plausible-sounding invention

feedback.vague: The answer wasn't vague — it was specific and confident. That's exactly the problem: a model avoiding liability would hedge, and this one didn't. The failure isn't caution, it's confident wrongness.
feedback.thin: Right. With little specific training text about this country's rules, the model reached for the closest well-represented pattern it had — a neighboring country's system — and produced the rest by completing a plausible shape, not by recalling a fact it had actually seen.

contentSections.mechanism: When a topic is thinly represented, a model doesn't fall back to silence or hedging by default — it falls back to pattern-completion from the nearest well-represented analog, blended with invented specifics that fit the shape of a real answer. The confidence of the output tracks the confidence of the completion process, not the reliability of the underlying facts.

contentSections.body: Thin data doesn't make an AI tool sound less sure of itself. It makes the tool more likely to blend in the nearest well-documented pattern — which is exactly why you have to know, yourself, when you're asking about something underrepresented.

title: How Bias Shows Up in Code, Not Just Prose
description: Variable names, example data, validation rules and assumed defaults an AI assistant writes into working code without being asked to think about any of it.

learningObjectives.text: Identify assumed defaults embedded in AI-generated code: example data, field validation, formatting
Explain why bias in generated code is easy to miss because the code still runs correctly
Revise a piece of AI-generated code to remove an unstated demographic or regional assumption

contentSections.title: It still compiles — that's the problem

contentSections.body: You ask an AI assistant for seed data to test a new user table: `{name: "John Smith", gender: "male", phone: "(555) 123-4567"}`, times twenty rows, almost all Anglo names, a gender field that's a two-value dropdown, every phone number in the North American format. It runs. Every test passes. Nothing about the code is broken. And every one of those choices is an assumption nobody asked for and the tests will never catch, because the tests were written against the same assumptions.

contentSections.scenario: You ask an AI assistant to "add a gender field to the user signup form." It generates: `<select name="gender"><option>Male</option><option>Female</option></select>`, required, no other options.
contentSections.question: What kind of default is this?

options.label: A bug — the code is technically incorrect
An assumed default — technically correct, functionally exclusionary for anyone outside the two options

feedback.bug: There's no syntax error and no crash — this is code a reviewer would approve without a second look, which is exactly why it's the dangerous kind of problem, not the obvious kind.
feedback.assumed: Right. It compiles, it validates, it ships. The exclusion is a design decision nobody made on purpose — a binary dropdown was simply the most common shape for "gender field" in the training data, so that's what got written when the prompt didn't specify otherwise.

contentSections.concept: Code-level bias is almost never a bug you can point a linter at. It's a working, tested, shippable default that quietly encodes an assumption — about names, genders, address formats, currencies, or family structures — that nobody in the room decided on purpose.

contentSections.body:
This shows up in a handful of recurring places, worth knowing by name because they're where you should actually look:

- **Example and seed data.** Sample names, addresses, and photos in generated test data or documentation default to whatever's most common in the training text — which, per the last lesson, is not evenly distributed.
- **Validation rules.** Phone number regexes that only accept North American formats, postal code patterns that assume 5-digit US ZIP codes, name fields that reject anything without a space (breaking single-name conventions used in several cultures) or reject non-Latin characters entirely.
- **Enum and dropdown values.** Binary gender fields, marital-status lists that don't include "domestic partnership," title dropdowns (Mr./Mrs./Ms.) with no option to skip.
- **Formatting assumptions.** Currency symbols, date formats (`MM/DD/YYYY` vs. the more common-globally `DD/MM/YYYY`), measurement units, and timezones defaulted without being asked.
- **Variable and function names.** Things like `is_male` as a boolean instead of a nullable or multi-value field — a naming choice that then constrains every piece of logic built on top of it, long after anyone remembers it was a default rather than a requirement.

None of this throws an error. It ships, it passes review, and it becomes the shape of the system — which is exactly why catching it is a deliberate reading habit, not something your test suite will do for you.

contentSections.title: Reading a snippet for what it assumed

contentSections.body: A working snippet doesn't announce its assumptions. Finding them means reading code you'd normally skim past, specifically looking for the places where a value had to come from somewhere and nobody in the prompt said where.

steps.label: Read the comment before the regex
steps.work: The assistant's own comment says "US/Canada format" — it named its assumption, which is more transparent than most generated code, and worth noticing precisely because it's rare.
steps.why: Most assumed defaults ship with no comment at all. When one is labeled, that's a gift — take it as a prompt to ask "was that actually the requirement, or just what filled the gap?"

steps.label: Check what the prompt actually specified
steps.work: The original request was "add phone number validation to the signup form" — nothing about which country or countries the product serves.
steps.why: If the product is US-only by design, this code is fine and the comment is just good documentation. If the product has, or wants, any international users, this is a silent scope limitation nobody decided on.

steps.label: Trace the actual failure mode
steps.work: A user with a UK, Kenyan, or Japanese phone number enters their real number and gets rejected as "invalid," with no explanation that the form is US/Canada-only.
steps.why: This is what makes it worse than a cosmetic gap: it produces a wrong error message. The user is told their real, correctly-formatted number is invalid, which is actively misleading, not just unhelpfully narrow.

steps.label: Decide the fix, not just flag the problem
steps.work: Either scope it honestly ("US/Canada numbers only" stated in the UI, if that's a real product constraint) or replace the regex with a library like libphonenumber that handles international formats, and change the error message to name what's actually wrong when it does reject something.
steps.why: "This is biased" isn't a fix. The fix is either an honest, stated scope decision or an actual internationalization change — and which one is right depends on the product, not on the code.

blanks.prompt: What assumption did the assistant name in its own comment?
blanks.why: Same pattern as the phone example — the comment names the default. Most of the world reads dates as day/month/year, so this format is a US-specific choice presented as if it were just "the" date format.

blanks.prompt: What's the actual failure a non-US user hits — not a crash, but what do they see?
blanks.answer: ambiguous or misread dates, e.g. 03/04/2025 read as 3 April instead of 4 March
blanks.why: This one is worse than the phone case in a specific way: it doesn't reject anything, so nobody gets an error to notice. A UK user reads 03/04/2025 as 3 April; the system meant 4 March. The order gets confirmed against the wrong date, silently.

blanks.prompt: What's the more defensible default for a checkout form with no stated regional scope? (name the format)
blanks.answer: an unambiguous format like YYYY-MM-DD, or a locale-aware formatter
blanks.why: ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD) is unambiguous regardless of the reader's locale, which is exactly the property this function needs and doesn't have. A locale-aware formatting library is the fuller fix if the product needs to *display* dates in the user's own convention.

contentSections.procedure: **Read the comment for a named assumption → check what the prompt actually specified → trace what a user outside that assumption actually experiences → decide a real fix, not just a flag.** Silent, un-erroring failures (the date bug) are worse than loud rejections (the phone bug), because nobody gets told anything went wrong.

contentSections.body: The dangerous version of this isn't the code that crashes — it's the code that runs cleanly, passes review, and quietly tells some of your users their correct information is invalid, or silently misreads it.

title: Why 'The Model Said So' Isn't Neutral
description: Reading an AI-generated recommendation critically instead of treating an AI's answer as an outside, unbiased opinion.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a model's recommendation carries the biases of the historical outcomes it learned to predict as 'good'
Evaluate an AI-generated recommendation for the historical pattern it's likely reproducing

contentSections.title: The recommendation and the pattern behind it

contentSections.body: A hiring manager asks an AI tool to "rank these five candidate summaries by fit for a senior engineering role." The tool ranks them, with reasoning that sounds sharp and specific for each one. The manager feels reassured — the ranking came from an outside, unbiased system, not their own gut. It didn't. It came from a pattern trained on which resumes historically correlated with being hired and rated well for similar roles — a history that has its own well-documented skew in exactly the field being ranked.

"The model said so" sounds like it should mean *an independent check on human judgment.* It usually means the opposite: **the model's ranking is a compressed summary of whatever pattern of past outcomes it learned to associate with success** — and if those past outcomes were shaped by human bias (in hiring, lending, admissions, medical triage, performance review, anything with a historical track record), the model reproduces that bias faithfully, confidently, and without disclosing that it's doing so.

The part that makes this genuinely dangerous rather than just imperfect: a biased human recommendation usually comes with a name attached, a person you can push back on, ask "why do you think that," and hold accountable. A model's ranking arrives with none of that — just a confident-sounding paragraph of reasoning that was generated *after* the ranking, to justify it, not derived independently and then used to produce it. It's easy to mistake that fluent justification for a rigorous process.

contentSections.scenario: An AI hiring-assistant tool consistently ranks candidates with a multi-year employment gap lower, even when the reasoning it gives each time is generic ("suggests potential inconsistency in work history") and never engages with the specific reason for the gap listed on the resume.
contentSections.question: What's driving that pattern?

options.label: The tool has verified that employment gaps genuinely predict worse job performance

Employment gaps correlated with lower hire/promotion rates in the historical data the tool learned from — a correlation shaped by whose gaps (caregiving, illness, disability) got penalized by human decision-makers, not by any real performance signal

feedback.verified: There's no mechanism by which the tool could have verified this — it wasn't given performance outcomes to check against, only resume patterns and historical hiring decisions to imitate. It learned a correlation, not a causal finding.
feedback.historical: Right. The tool is reproducing a historical hiring pattern, and employment gaps are disproportionately tied to caregiving, chronic illness, and disability — meaning the 'signal' it learned is largely a record of who got screened out for reasons that had nothing to do with their actual ability to do the job.

contentSections.mechanism: A ranking model trained on historical outcomes doesn't know why those outcomes happened — it only knows that they correlated with certain resume features. When the training outcomes were themselves produced by biased human decisions, the model learns to reproduce the bias as if it were a genuine predictor of quality, and states it with exactly the same confidence it would use for a real one.

contentSections.body: A model's recommendation isn't an outside check on bias — it's a compressed record of whatever pattern of past decisions it learned to imitate, including the bias in those decisions, delivered with no disclosure that it's doing so.

contentSections.title: "Ignore demographics" doesn't work the way it sounds like it should

contentSections.body:
A common, well-intentioned fix is telling the model: "Rank these candidates on merit only — ignore race, gender, age, and other demographic factors." It's worth understanding precisely why this instruction does less than it sounds like it does.

Even with an explicit instruction not to use demographic factors, a model can still pick up **proxies** — signals that correlate with demographic categories without naming them directly. A candidate's name can correlate with ethnicity. A graduation year can correlate with age. A neighborhood or school district in an address can correlate with race and class. A resume gap can correlate with caregiving status or disability. None of those are the literal words "female" or "over 50" — so an instruction to "ignore demographic factors" doesn't reliably stop the model from weighing them anyway, because it was never told *those specific fields* were the proxies doing the work.

contentSections.question: A hiring tool is told "ignore demographic factors" and then given two otherwise-identical resumes that differ only in the candidate's home zip code. Will its ranking of the two candidates necessarily come out identical?
contentSections.answer: **Not necessarily.** Zip code wasn't named in the instruction, but it correlates with race and class in many regions — the tool was never told this specific field was a proxy, so nothing stops it from weighing the correlation it learned from historical data, even while faithfully avoiding the literal demographic terms it was told to ignore.
contentSections.hint: The instruction named categories like race and gender by name. Was zip code one of the named categories?

contentSections.body: This doesn't mean the instruction is worthless — it can measurably reduce some effects. It means it's not a fix you can trust blindly, and the honest response to "we told it to be objective" is "okay, and did you actually test that, on cases where you know the right answer?"

Telling a model to ignore demographics stops it from using the literal words — it doesn't reliably stop it from using the proxies that carry the same information. Treat "we told it to be objective" as a claim to test, not a fix to trust.

title: What Fixing Bias in a Deployed System Actually Involves, and Its Limits
description: The real process behind 'we fixed the bias' — and why that sentence should raise your eyebrows about as much as 'we fixed security.'

learningObjectives.text: Sequence the real steps involved in addressing a specific bias finding in a deployed AI system
Explain why bias mitigation is partial and ongoing rather than a one-time fix

contentSections.title: "We fixed it" is doing a lot of work in that sentence

contentSections.body: An early image-generation tool, criticized for defaulting historical scenes to all-white casts, was updated to diversify people in generated images. Soon after, it was generating racially diverse depictions of specific historical figures and groups where that diversity was factually wrong for the scene requested. The team hadn't found the fix — they'd found a different, more visible failure mode. Bias mitigation doesn't have a finish line; it has trade-offs you have to keep watching.

Fixing a specific, documented bias in a deployed system is real, worthwhile work — and it's also narrower and more ongoing than "we fixed the bias" makes it sound. The actual process looks like:

1. **Document the specific failure** with concrete evidence — not "the model seems biased" but "here are twelve outputs, here's the pattern, here's who it affects."
2. **Build an evaluation set** of similar cases, so you have a way to measure whether an intervention actually helps *before* you ship it, rather than eyeballing a few examples.
3. **Try interventions at the right layer** — this can mean adjusting the system prompt, fine-tuning on more balanced examples, adding a post-processing filter, or in some cases deciding the tool shouldn't be used for that task at all.
4. **Measure against the eval set for improvement without new regressions** — an intervention that fixes the documented case but introduces the over-correction problem from the hook above hasn't fixed anything, it's traded one bias for a different, sometimes worse, one.
5. **Keep monitoring in production**, because new failure cases surface constantly, from users doing things the eval set never anticipated.

Notice what's not on this list: a step where the bias is gone and monitoring stops. There isn't one.

contentSections.question: Put the real process for addressing a documented bias finding in order.
steps: Document the specific failure with concrete evidence and who it affects
Build an evaluation set of similar cases to measure against
Try an intervention at the appropriate layer (prompting, fine-tuning, filtering, or scoping the tool out of the task)
Measure the intervention against the eval set for improvement without new regressions
Keep monitoring in production, because new failure cases will surface
contentSections.explanation: Running this out of order — trying an intervention before you've documented the specific failure, or shipping without an eval set to check for regressions — is how a team ends up trading one visible bias for a less-visible one, the way the diversify-everything image fix did.

contentSections.body: A real bias fix targets a documented, specific failure, gets measured against an eval set for new regressions, and then keeps being monitored — because there's no step where the work is done.

contentSections.title: What this means for you as a user, not just a builder

contentSections.body:
Most people using an AI tool aren't the ones who can run that five-step process — that's product-team work. But knowing what real mitigation actually involves changes what you should expect from claims about it.

**"We fixed the bias" is a claim about one documented case, not a guarantee about every future one.** A tool that improved on a specific, publicized failure hasn't become unbiased in general — it's had one measured intervention against one eval set. Treat the claim the way you'd treat "we fixed the security vulnerability" after one CVE: true and worth something, and not a reason to stop checking.

contentSections.question: A vendor announces they fixed a widely-reported bias issue in their hiring tool. You noticed a related but not identical pattern in your own use of the tool a few months ago. Does the announcement mean your specific pattern is now resolved too?
contentSections.answer: **Not necessarily.** The announced fix was measured against an eval set built around the publicized case. A related-but-different pattern you noticed independently may not be represented in that eval set at all, so the improvement it demonstrates doesn't automatically transfer to it — worth re-checking your own case rather than assuming.
contentSections.hint: What did the eval set in the five-step process actually get built around — every possible case, or the one that was documented?

contentSections.body: **Your own vigilance doesn't stop being useful once a vendor says they've addressed something.** If you noticed a bias pattern in a tool you use regularly, checking whether it's actually gone — on your own use case, not just the publicized one — is still worth the two minutes it takes, because the fix that worked on the eval set doesn't automatically generalize to your specific context.
"Fixed" means one documented case got a measured intervention — not that the underlying tendency is gone. Keep checking your own use case even after a vendor announces a fix.

title: Practice — Spot the Biased Default in Eight AI Outputs
description: Eight drills recognizing where a default came from and what it predicts. No new concepts — this is where noticing an assumed default stops being something you read about.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the training-data-skew explanation to unfamiliar AI outputs at speed
Classify a biased default by its source: demographic skew, thin regional data, or an unstated assumption in code

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or spread across three — nothing is timed and nothing expires.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Audit an AI Tool's Output for a Specific Underrepresented Case
description: Pick a real AI tool and a real underrepresented case, run it, and write the finding the way a practitioner would — not a complaint, a documented pattern with a mitigation.

learningObjectives.text: Design a small, repeatable test of an AI tool's output on a specific underrepresented case
Produce a written finding that names the assumption, who it excludes, and a concrete mitigation

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the actual first step of the five-step mitigation process from lesson five, run for real: document one specific failure with concrete evidence. That's a skill worth having on its own, independent of whether you're ever the person who fixes it — being able to hand a team a well-documented finding instead of a vague complaint is what makes the difference land.

contentSections.title: Audit finding: a specific underrepresented case
contentSections.brief: Pick one AI tool you can actually run (a chat assistant, a code assistant, an image generator, a resume screener, whatever you have access to) and one specific, underrepresented case relevant to it — a name, a region, a disability, a family structure, a language, a job history pattern. Run it, more than once, and document what you find the way a practitioner would document a real finding: specific, evidenced, and useful to whoever would fix it.
contentSections.deliverable: A written finding: what the model assumed, who that assumption excludes, and one concrete mitigation — specific enough that someone could act on it without asking you follow-up questions.

stages.title: Pick the tool and the case, and run it
stages.instructions: Choose one AI tool and one specific underrepresented case from the lessons (or a real one from your own life or work). Write the exact prompt or task you'll give it, then run it at least three times — varying only the detail that shouldn't matter (rephrasing, running it twice, or a near-identical second case) to check whether the pattern is consistent or a one-off. Save every output, not just the most striking one.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least three saved outputs from the same tool, on the same or closely related case, with the exact prompts you used.

stages.title: Name what the model assumed and who it excludes
stages.instructions: Looking at what you saved, write down precisely what the tool defaulted to when it had room to guess, and use lessons one through three to identify why: demographic skew in training text, thin regional/topic data, or an unstated assumption baked into example data or validation logic. Then name, specifically, who that default excludes or underserves — not "some users," but the actual group and the actual cost to them (rejected input, wrong information, invisibility in the output, or something else).
stages.checkpoint: You can state the assumption in one sentence and the excluded group in one sentence, and both are specific enough that a stranger reading them would understand exactly what you found.

stages.title: Write the finding and one real mitigation
stages.instructions: Write the finding as you'd hand it to a team: what you tested, what you found (with the evidence), who it affects, and one concrete mitigation. A mitigation is concrete if it names an actual change — a rewritten prompt, a different validation rule, a system-prompt instruction, a note in documentation about the tool's known limitation — not "be more careful" or "train it on more diverse data," which aren't things a single user can act on. Then self-check your draft against the rubric below before calling it done.
stages.checkpoint: The finding names a specific assumption, a specific excluded group, and a mitigation someone could actually implement this week.

rubric.criterion: The case is specific, not generic
rubric.meets: Names a real tool, a real prompt or task, and a specific underrepresented case — not 'AI can be biased.'

rubric.criterion: The evidence is shown, not just claimed
rubric.meets: Includes at least the key excerpts from the saved outputs the finding is based on, not just a summary of what you remember.

rubric.criterion: The pattern was checked for consistency
rubric.meets: Ran the test more than once and reports whether the pattern held, rather than generalizing from a single output.

rubric.criterion: The excluded group is named concretely
rubric.meets: States who is affected and how, specifically enough that someone unfamiliar with the case understands the real-world cost.

rubric.criterion: The mitigation is actually actionable
rubric.meets: Names a specific change someone could make — not a general call for more training data or more care.

rubric.criterion: It reads like a finding, not a complaint
rubric.meets: Stated as documented fact with evidence, in the register you'd use handing this to a team that has to prioritize it.

contentSections.body: The gap between noticing a biased default and being able to document one well enough for someone else to act on it is most of what separates a passing complaint from a finding that gets fixed.

title: Checkpoint — Whose Defaults These Are
description: Ten questions pulling from this module. Ungraded, untimed — getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions about defaults and bias without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Whose Defaults These Are

questions.from: This module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: What does an AI model's 'default' answer actually consist of, mechanically?

options.label: The single most statistically common completion for an underspecified prompt in the training distribution
A deliberate choice made by the model's developers about what's typical
The objectively correct answer when no other detail is given

questions.explanation: It's a statistic about training text, surfaced when a prompt leaves room to guess — not a considered choice by anyone, and not evidence that the common case fits your situation.

questions.from: This module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: What happens to a model's confidence when it's answering about a topic thin in its training data?

options.label: It typically hedges more and sounds less certain
Its tone stays just as confident even as accuracy drops
It usually declines to answer at all

questions.explanation: Confidence doesn't track reliability of the underlying data. That gap between fluent tone and thin support is exactly why you have to know when you're asking about something underrepresented.

questions.from: This module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: Why does Wikipedia's training-text influence carry a specific skew, despite being a huge, high-quality source?

options.label: Its content is intentionally biased toward certain viewpoints
Its volunteer editor base skews toward a narrow demographic, which shapes framing and notability judgments
It isn't actually part of most models' training data

questions.explanation: It's an extraordinary volunteer project, and its editor base is still a narrow, documented slice of humanity — whose framing and gaps get carried into a large share of what a model treats as general knowledge.

questions.from: This module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: Which of these is most likely to be UNDERrepresented in a large model's web-scraped training text?

options.label: English-language software documentation
Knowledge traditionally passed on orally rather than published
US and UK news writing

questions.explanation: A model can only learn from what got written down and crawled. Oral knowledge traditions are largely absent from training text regardless of how central they are to the people who hold them.

questions.from: This module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: An AI-generated phone-number validator only accepts North American formats. What's the most accurate description of this?

options.label: A syntax bug that will crash on other input
A working, tested default that silently rejects real, correctly-formatted numbers from elsewhere
Not a real problem unless the product is explicitly international

questions.explanation: It compiles, validates, and ships clean — and tells users with real, correct numbers that their input is invalid. That combination (working code, wrong outcome) is what makes this kind of bias easy to miss.

questions.from: This module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: Why is a silent date-format bug (misreading 03/04 as the wrong date) worse in one specific way than a rejecting bug like the phone validator?

options.label: It affects more users overall
Nobody gets an error message, so nobody is prompted to notice anything went wrong
It's harder to fix technically

questions.explanation: The phone validator at least tells the user something's wrong. The date bug produces a wrong-but-plausible result with no error at all — the failure is invisible to everyone involved unless someone goes looking for it.

questions.from: This module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: An AI hiring tool ranks candidates with employment gaps lower, with generic reasoning that never engages the actual reason for the gap. What's really driving that ranking?

options.label: A verified finding that gaps predict worse job performance
A correlation learned from historical hiring decisions, which were themselves shaped by bias against caregivers and people with disabilities
A neutral statistical pattern with no connection to human bias

questions.explanation: The tool wasn't given performance outcomes to verify against — only historical hiring decisions to imitate, including whatever bias shaped those decisions.

questions.from: This module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: Why doesn't telling a model to 'ignore demographic factors' reliably remove demographic bias from its output?

options.label: The model ignores instructions it disagrees with
Proxies like name, address, or graduation year can carry the same information without using the literal demographic terms
The instruction only works for gender, not other categories

questions.explanation: An instruction not to use demographic words doesn't identify which ordinary-looking fields are acting as proxies for those categories — so the model can keep weighing them without ever touching a literal demographic term.

questions.from: This module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: What's missing from the real five-step process of fixing a documented bias in a deployed system?

options.label: A step where the fix is verified against an evaluation set
A final step where the bias is confirmed gone and monitoring stops
A step where the specific failure gets documented with evidence

questions.explanation: There isn't a finish line. New failure cases keep surfacing after any fix ships, which is why ongoing monitoring is part of the process rather than an afterthought.

questions.from: This module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: A vendor announces they've 'fixed' a publicized bias case in their tool. What's the reasonable response?

options.label: Treat it as evidence the tool is now unbiased in general
Treat it as one documented case with a measured intervention, and still check your own use case
Assume the claim is marketing and ignore it entirely

questions.explanation: It's true and worth something — the same way 'we fixed a CVE' is worth something — without being a guarantee that covers every future case, including yours specifically.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Where a Prompt Actually Goes After You Hit Send
description: The literal path a message takes once you submit it to an AI tool — and why 'it felt like typing into a private text box' is not evidence of anything.

learningObjectives.text: Describe the actual path a prompt takes from a user's device to a provider's infrastructure and back
Explain why the interface's appearance (a private-feeling chat box) is not evidence about data handling

contentSections.title: It feels private. It isn't local.

contentSections.body: A developer hits a confusing error at 11pm, pastes the full stack trace into an AI chat tool to debug it — including a database connection string sitting right there in the trace — and gets a fix in ten seconds. The chat box looked exactly like a text editor. It wasn't one. Everything typed into it left the machine.

When you send a prompt to an AI tool — a chat app, a code assistant plugged into your editor, an API call your own product makes — here's the actual path, not the felt one:

1. **Your text leaves your device** over the network, the same as any web request.
2. **It arrives at the provider's servers**, where the model itself runs. It is not processed on your laptop or phone, even when the interface is a native app that makes it feel local.
3. **It's typically logged**, at least briefly, for abuse monitoring and debugging — this is close to universal among AI providers and is a different thing from being used for training.
4. **It may or may not be used to improve future models**, depending on the specific product, account tier, and settings — covered in the next lesson.
5. **It may be retained** for some period — days, months, or until you delete your account — again depending on the specific product and plan.

None of this is unique to AI tools; it's how any client-server product works, including your email and your bank's website. What's different is how the interface *feels*. A chat window with your own message history scrolling above it reads like a private notebook. It's closer, structurally, to sending an email — legible to the operator of the service, logged somewhere, and not something you can un-send.

contentSections.question: Put the actual path of a prompt in order, from the moment you hit send.
steps: Text leaves your device over the network
It arrives at the provider's servers, where the model runs
It is logged, at least briefly, for abuse monitoring and debugging
It may be used to improve future models, depending on product and settings
It may be retained for some period, depending on product and plan
contentSections.explanation: Notice logging for abuse monitoring happens close to universally and is separate from the training-use question — a product that promises "we don't train on your data" hasn't necessarily promised "we don't log it at all." Those are two different commitments, and the next lesson is about telling them apart.

contentSections.body: A prompt leaves your device, is processed and typically logged on someone else's infrastructure, and is not something you can un-send — regardless of how private the interface makes it feel.

contentSections.title: "It can't be un-sent" is the load-bearing fact

contentSections.body: You paste a paragraph into an AI tool, immediately realize it contained something sensitive, and delete it from the chat window a second later. The chat window is now clean. The request already left your device before you deleted anything — the delete removed it from your screen, not from wherever it already arrived.

contentSections.question: A user pastes a client's phone number into an AI chat tool, then immediately deletes the message from the visible chat history before the AI responds. Has the risk been avoided?
contentSections.answer: **No.** The request had already left the device and reached the provider's servers before the message was deleted from the visible history. Deleting it from the interface removes it from what you can see, not from what was already transmitted and potentially logged.
contentSections.hint: Think about the order of operations: does hitting send happen before or after the request reaches the server?

contentSections.body:
This is the single fact worth carrying out of this lesson, because it's the one that changes behavior: **the moment of risk is the moment you hit send, not any moment after.** Deleting a message from a chat history, closing the tab, or clearing local storage does nothing to a request that already reached a server. There is no 'undo' for a prompt the way there's an undo for a typo.

That doesn't mean every AI tool is a trap, or that you should stop using them for anything sensitive-adjacent. It means the decision has to happen *before* you hit send, not after — which is exactly the skill the rest of this module builds toward: knowing, in the moment, what's actually safe to type.
The decision point is before you hit send. Nothing you do afterward — deleting the message, closing the tab — reaches back and un-transmits it.

title: What Providers Do and Don't Do With Your Data, and How to Actually Check
description: A four-question framework for reading any AI provider's actual data policy instead of assuming one, plus why the answer differs by account tier for the same company.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a four-question framework to determine an AI provider's actual data handling for a given account
Explain why the same company can have different data-handling defaults for different account tiers

contentSections.title: The same company, two different answers

contentSections.body: A freelancer uses the free consumer version of an AI chat app for client work, and separately, their client's company has an enterprise agreement with the same provider for internal use. Both are talking to the same underlying model. Their data is very likely handled under different rules — different training-use defaults, possibly different retention windows — because the account tier, not the model, is what the policy attaches to.

It's tempting to treat "what does this company do with data" as one fact you learn once. It usually isn't. The same provider commonly runs multiple products or tiers — a free consumer app, a paid consumer subscription, a business/team plan, an API for developers, an enterprise contract — and the data-handling terms are frequently different across them, sometimes significantly. A free consumer tier is disproportionately likely to use conversations to improve future models by default (with an opt-out you may have to find and enable yourself); an API or enterprise agreement is more likely to default the other way, sometimes with a contractual commitment not to train on your data at all.

This means "Company X says they don't train on user data" is often true of one product and false of another from the exact same company — so the check has to be specific to the actual product and tier you're using, not the brand name.

contentSections.scenario: A person reads a news article stating that "Provider X doesn't use customer data to train its models" and concludes it's safe to paste anything into Provider X's free consumer chat app.
contentSections.question: What's the gap in that reasoning?

options.label: The article was probably describing the provider's enterprise/API terms, which don't automatically apply to the free consumer product
There's no gap — if the company says it, it applies everywhere they operate

feedback.none: Company-wide statements usually describe a specific product or contract, most often the enterprise/API terms where the strongest commitments tend to live — not a blanket promise covering every free consumer surface the same company also runs.
feedback.tier: Right. Data-handling terms attach to the specific product and account tier, not the company as a whole. The free consumer chat app and the enterprise contract can, and often do, have different defaults even though it's the same underlying model and the same company name.

contentSections.concept: A data-handling claim is only as reliable as the specific product it was made about. Always match the claim to the tier you're actually using, not the brand.

contentSections.body: The same company can have meaningfully different data rules across its free, paid, and enterprise products — check the tier you're actually on, not the headline about the brand.

contentSections.title: Four questions to actually check

contentSections.body:
Instead of trying to remember a policy, run this four-question check against the specific tool and account tier you're using, whenever it matters — this takes a few minutes on the provider's actual privacy or data-usage page, not a guess from memory:

1. **Is training on my data the default, or opt-in, or opt-out — and where's the toggle?** Free consumer tiers frequently default to "on" for training use, with an opt-out buried in settings. Paid or business tiers frequently default the other way.
2. **What's the retention window for logs kept for abuse/safety monitoring?** This exists close to universally and is separate from training use — a "we don't train on your data" promise doesn't necessarily mean "we don't retain it at all."
3. **Does my account tier come with a specific contractual commitment**, or just a general policy statement? A contract (common in enterprise/API agreements) is a stronger commitment than a policy page a company could revise unilaterally.
4. **Who at my organization controls this setting, if it's a workplace account?** An individual employee often can't change an org-wide data setting — that's an admin decision, worth knowing before assuming your own preference is what's actually in effect.

contentSections.question: You want to know whether your team's AI coding assistant trains on the code you paste into it. Where's the most reliable place to find the actual, current answer?
contentSections.answer: **The provider's own data-usage or privacy page for the specific product and tier you're on** — checked now, not remembered from a blog post or a colleague's guess from a year ago. Policies change, tiers change, and a secondhand summary is often about a different product than the one you're actually using.
contentSections.hint: Think about which source is specific to your exact product and tier, and current as of today.

contentSections.body: Four questions, checked on the actual product page, for the actual tier you're on: training default, retention window, contractual versus policy-only, and who controls the setting if it's an org account.

title: Categories of Data That Should Never Go in a Prompt
description: Secrets, PII, and regulated data — three categories worth recognizing on sight, because the cost of getting them wrong doesn't scale down with how innocent the request felt.

learningObjectives.text: Classify a piece of data as a secret, PII, regulated data, or none of those, and justify the classification
Identify the specific harm each category risks if sent to a third-party AI tool

contentSections.title: Three categories, three different harms

contentSections.body: A developer debugging a failed API call pastes their entire `.env` file into an AI chat to "double check the config," including a live secret key — the kind that starts with a recognizable live-mode prefix and grants real account access. The bug gets fixed in one reply. The key is now sitting in a chat log on infrastructure the developer doesn't control, and the only real fix left is rotating it.

Three categories are worth recognizing on sight, because each risks a different, specific harm:

**Secrets and credentials** — API keys, passwords, tokens, database connection strings, private SSH keys. The harm is direct and immediate: whoever has access to that text now has access to whatever the credential unlocks. There's no partial version of this risk — a leaked key is a leaked key, full stop, and the only real remedy is rotating it, not hoping it wasn't noticed.

**Personally identifiable information (PII)** — full names combined with any identifying detail: email, phone, government ID, home address, date of birth. The harm here is about a real person's exposure, not yours — you're making a decision about someone else's data, often without their knowledge or consent, which is a meaningfully different thing from risking your own information.

**Regulated data** — health records (PHI), financial account details (PCI-scope data), legally privileged communications. The harm compounds: beyond the exposure itself, there can be real legal and regulatory consequences for the organization that let it happen, on top of the personal harm to whoever's data it was.

contentSections.scenario: You're about to paste something into a third-party AI tool to get help with it.
contentSections.question: Select every item that falls into one of the three never-send categories from this lesson.

items.label: A live API key, even truncated to just its prefix for context
A patient's clinical notes, including diagnosis and medication
A spreadsheet of customer names, emails, and purchase history
Your own résumé, to get feedback on the writing
A snippet from your own public open-source repository
A generic error message with no identifying data in it

explanation.api-key: Never — even a truncated key can be enough to identify which service and account it belongs to, and the safe move is describing it in prose ("a live key with such-and-such prefix") rather than pasting any real characters at all.
explanation.patient-notes: Never — regulated data (PHI). This is true even if you're the patient's own developer trying to debug the system that stores it; the sensitivity of the content doesn't change based on who's asking.
explanation.customer-list: Never as-is — PII belonging to other people, who didn't consent to having their data sent to a third-party AI tool. This is a decision about someone else's exposure, not just your own risk tolerance.
explanation.own-résumé: Fine — it's your own information, offered voluntarily, for a purpose you control.
explanation.public-repo: Fine — you already chose to make this public; nothing about sending it to an AI tool changes its exposure.
explanation.generic-error: Fine — genuinely generic technical content with nothing identifying attached carries none of the three categories' risks.

contentSections.synthesis: The test isn't "does this feel sensitive" — it's a specific check: is this a secret (direct access risk), someone else's identifying information (their exposure, not yours to trade away), or data under a specific regulatory regime (PHI, PCI, legal privilege)? If none of the three apply and it's your own information or already public, you're clear.

contentSections.body: Secrets, other people's PII, and regulated data are three different harms with one shared property: the cost doesn't scale down just because the request that leaked them felt small and innocent.

contentSections.title: The pattern that makes people miss it

contentSections.body:
The realistic failure isn't someone deliberately deciding to paste a customer database into an AI tool. It's pasting a whole file, log, or export to solve one narrow problem and not noticing what else came along with it. A `.env` file pasted for one config question brings every other secret in the file with it. A support ticket pasted to "help me write a better response" brings the customer's full name and account details along with the one sentence you actually needed help rephrasing.

The practical habit that catches most of this: **before pasting a whole block of anything, ask what you actually need the AI to see, and paste only that** — not the file, the ticket, or the export, but the specific lines the task requires. This single habit prevents most of the accidental-inclusion cases that don't feel like a privacy decision at all in the moment.

contentSections.code:
Prompt sent to an AI writing assistant:

"Help me write a friendlier reply to this support ticket:

---
Ticket #48291
From: Sarah Chen (sarah.chen@email.example, +1-555-0148)
Account: Premium, since 2019
Issue: My order #77821 arrived damaged, and I'm frustrated because 
this is the second time this month.
---

My draft reply: 'We apologize for the inconvenience...'"
contentSections.question: What's the actual problem with this prompt?

options.label: The draft reply is too generic and the AI won't be able to improve it
The whole ticket — including the customer's name, email, and phone number — was pasted when only the issue description was needed to rewrite the reply
Nothing is wrong; support tickets are internal business data, not personal data

feedback.generic: That might also be true, but it's not the problem this lesson is about — the prompt would work exactly as well for rewriting tone with the identifying fields removed.
feedback.overinclude: Right. Rewriting the tone of a reply doesn't require the customer's name, email, or phone number — only the issue description does. Everything else was pasted along for the ride because it was easier than trimming it.
feedback.internal: A support ticket containing a named customer's contact details is exactly PII, regardless of which system it lives in — 'internal' describes who can normally see it, not whether it's identifying information about a real person.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A usable version: "Help me write a friendlier reply to this support message: 'My order arrived damaged, and this is the second time this month, I'm frustrated.' My draft reply: '...'" Same task, same result, none of the customer's identifying information anywhere in the prompt.

contentSections.body: Most leaks aren't a decision to share something sensitive — they're pasting a whole block when only a fragment was needed. Paste only what the task actually requires.

title: Enterprise and 'Zero Data Retention' Modes — What They Actually Change
description: What an enterprise agreement or a zero-data-retention setting really commits a provider to, and the specific things it does not fix.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a zero-data-retention or enterprise agreement typically commits a provider to
Identify what an enterprise or ZDR setting does not change about existing risk

contentSections.title: What the upgrade actually buys you

contentSections.body: A company moves from a team plan to an enterprise agreement with their AI provider, partly because "zero data retention" sounds like the privacy problem is now solved. An employee still pastes a client's unreleased financial results into a prompt to "summarize the highlights for a slide." ZDR changes what happens to that text after it's processed. It does not change whether that text should have been sent at all.

"Zero data retention" (ZDR) and enterprise agreements typically commit a provider to some combination of: not using your organization's data to train models, deleting request content shortly after processing rather than retaining it, and sometimes a contractual guarantee (not just a policy statement) backing those commitments. These are real, meaningful upgrades over a default consumer tier — the difference between a company's general policy page (which it can revise) and a signed agreement specific to your organization is not a small one.

What it does *not* do: it doesn't retroactively apply to anything sent before the setting was turned on. It doesn't change abuse and safety monitoring obligations, which most providers maintain some minimal version of regardless of retention settings, for legal and platform-safety reasons. It doesn't extend automatically to every tool your organization uses — a ZDR setting on the main chat product doesn't cover a separate plugin, integration, or a different tier an individual employee might be using on the side. And most importantly: **it doesn't change whether a piece of information should have been sent to a third party at all.** ZDR changes what happens to data after transmission. It says nothing about whether transmitting it was the right call in the first place.

contentSections.scenario: An employee at a company with a zero-data-retention enterprise agreement pastes an unreleased product roadmap into the company's AI chat tool to get help summarizing it, reasoning "we're on ZDR, so this is fine."
contentSections.question: What's the actual gap in that reasoning?

options.label: ZDR guarantees the AI provider's employees will never see the content under any circumstances
ZDR is a commitment about what happens to data after it's transmitted and processed — it says nothing about whether sending confidential business content to any third party was the right call

feedback.never-see: ZDR commitments are usually about not retaining or training on data, not an absolute guarantee that literally no human or system process ever touches it — abuse monitoring, for instance, typically still applies in some limited form.
feedback.transmission: Right. ZDR governs what happens after the data arrives — not whether an unreleased roadmap should have left the building for a third party's servers at all. Those are two separate questions, and ZDR only answers the second one.

contentSections.mechanism: Data-handling settings like ZDR reduce what a provider does with data once it's received. They don't reduce the initial exposure of transmitting it in the first place, and they don't substitute for a judgment about whether the content was appropriate to send anywhere outside the organization to begin with.

contentSections.body: Enterprise and ZDR settings are real, meaningful commitments about what happens after data is transmitted. They are not a judgment call about whether the data should have been transmitted, and they don't apply retroactively or automatically to every tool you touch.

contentSections.title: Whose setting is it, actually

contentSections.body: One more gap worth naming plainly: an individual employee usually doesn't control the organization's data-handling settings, and often doesn't know exactly what they are. "My company has an enterprise agreement" is a fact about the organization's contract — it isn't the same as "I personally know this setting is correctly configured for the specific tool I'm using right now."

contentSections.question: You're at work and want to use a free browser extension that adds AI features to your email client — separate from your company's official, enterprise-configured AI chat tool. Is it safe to assume the extension is covered by the same enterprise agreement?
contentSections.answer: **No — assume it isn't, until confirmed otherwise.** An enterprise agreement covers the specific product it names. A separate extension, even one used on a work device for work tasks, is very likely a different product entirely, under its own (possibly consumer-default) data terms.
contentSections.hint: The enterprise agreement was negotiated for a named product. Is a separately-installed browser extension that product?

contentSections.body: A practical habit: if you're using an AI tool through work and you're not sure whether it's the enterprise-configured version or a consumer tier an employee could also technically reach, treat it as if it's the less protected one until you've actually confirmed otherwise. The assumption that costs you nothing if you're wrong is the cautious one — the assumption that costs you something if you're wrong is assuming protection you haven't verified.

An organization having an enterprise agreement is a fact about a contract, not a guarantee about the specific tool in front of you right now. When you're not sure which one you're using, assume the less protected one until you've checked.

title: A Personal Rule for What You Will and Won't Paste Into an AI Tool
description: A rule that survives being applied at 11pm under deadline pressure, not one that only works when you have time to think it through.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a candidate personal rule for whether it can actually be applied quickly, under pressure, without lookup
State a personal rule for what to send to a third-party AI tool that covers the categories from this module

contentSections.title: A rule you have to look up isn't a rule

contentSections.body: Someone reads this entire module carefully, nodding along, then three weeks later is debugging a production issue at 11pm, under real pressure, and pastes a full error log — customer emails and all — into an AI chat without a second thought. Not because they forgot the module existed. Because the module gave them categories to recognize, not a fast enough test to run in the two seconds before hitting send.

Everything in this module so far has been about recognizing categories — secrets, PII, regulated data, tier differences. That's necessary and it's not sufficient, because recognizing a category takes longer than the moment you actually have to decide in. What you need for the actual moment is a rule short enough to run without conscious effort, the way you don't consciously think through traffic rules at every intersection.

A workable personal rule has three properties: it's a **small number of yes/no questions** (not a lookup table), it's phrased around **what you're about to paste**, not an abstract category (so you don't have to first classify something before applying the rule to it), and it **defaults to caution** when you're unsure or moving fast, because the moments you're most likely to skip the check are exactly the moments you're tired or rushed.

contentSections.scenario: Most people who read a module like this one and then get asked, a month later, whether they still consciously run through the categories before pasting something sensitive into an AI tool.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share say they still consciously think it through every time, rather than having it become closer to automatic (or having stopped thinking about it at all)?
contentSections.explanation: Low — and that's not a failure of the reader, it's a realistic description of how habits work. Conscious deliberation is expensive and doesn't survive fatigue or urgency. The design goal of a personal rule isn't to keep the deliberation alive forever — it's to compress it into something fast enough to survive being tired, which is a different, more achievable target.

contentSections.body: A rule that only works when you have time to carefully think it through will fail exactly when you need it most. Design for the tired, rushed version of yourself, not the careful one reading this lesson.

contentSections.title: Writing your own

contentSections.body:
Here's one worked example of a fast, three-question rule — not the only correct answer, but a template for the shape yours should take:

> **Before pasting:** (1) Could this identify a specific real person who isn't me? (2) Would I be upset if this appeared in a data breach headline tomorrow? (3) Is this actually mine to share — or someone else's information, a client's confidential document, an employer's unreleased plan? If any answer is yes-that's-a-problem, don't paste it raw. Either paste less (only the fragment the task needs), replace identifying details with placeholders, or don't use this tool for this task.

contentSections.question: Someone proposes this personal rule: "I'll check the provider's privacy policy before pasting anything sensitive." What's the practical problem with this specific rule, even though the instinct behind it is right?
contentSections.answer: **It's not fast enough to survive real use.** Reading a privacy policy takes minutes, not seconds — which means it's exactly the kind of check that gets skipped the moment you're rushed or tired, i.e. precisely the moments this module keeps pointing to as the highest-risk ones. The instinct (check before you paste) is right; the specific mechanism is too slow to actually run.
contentSections.hint: Think about how long reading a privacy policy actually takes, compared to the moment you're standing in when you're about to hit send.

contentSections.body: The categories from this module are what a good rule has to cover. The rule itself has to be short enough to survive being tired — write it that way, or it won't be there when it matters.

title: Practice — Judge Seven Prompts for What They Leak
