learningObjectives.text: Apply the never-send categories and the paste-only-what's-needed habit to unfamiliar prompts at speed
Distinguish a genuinely risky prompt from one that looks sensitive but isn't

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven prompts, judged the way you'd actually judge your own before hitting send. Do them in one sitting or spread out — nothing here is timed.
If you hesitated on one of these, that hesitation is useful information about where your own rule needs to be more specific.

title: Lab — Rewrite Three Risky Real Prompts to Remove Sensitive Data
description: Take three prompts you'd realistically write, find exactly what's sensitive in each, and rewrite them so they're still useful without the risk.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific sensitive content in a realistic prompt versus what the task actually requires
Rewrite a risky prompt to remove sensitive data while preserving its usefulness

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: The gap between knowing the categories and actually rewriting a real prompt under them is bigger than it looks — it's the same gap between knowing grammar rules and being able to edit a paragraph fast. This lab is the second one, done three times on prompts close enough to your real work that the skill transfers.

contentSections.title: Three before/after prompt rewrites
contentSections.brief: Find or recall three prompts you would realistically write for real work or personal use — not hypothetical ones. At least one should involve something from this module's never-send categories (a secret, someone else's PII, or regulated data), and the other two can be milder, real judgment calls. For each, produce a rewritten version that keeps the task useful while removing what shouldn't have been sent.
contentSections.deliverable: Three before/after prompt pairs, each with a short note on exactly what was removed and why the after-version is still just as useful for the actual task.

stages.title: Collect three real prompts and flag what's risky
stages.instructions: Write out three prompts close to ones you'd actually send — from your own work, a hypothetical based on a real situation you've been in, or adapted from this module's examples. For each, mark specifically what's risky: is it a secret, someone else's PII, regulated data, or an org-confidential detail? Be precise — 'this whole thing feels risky' isn't a flag, 'the customer's email and phone number in paragraph two' is.
stages.checkpoint: Each of the three prompts has a specific, named risk (or confirmed low risk) rather than a vague sense of unease.

stages.title: Rewrite each one
stages.instructions: For each prompt, produce a rewritten version using the techniques from this module: trim to only the fragment the task needs, replace identifying details with roles or placeholders, generalize specifics that don't need to be exact. Check each rewrite against one test: would the AI tool still be able to do the actual task you need, using only the after-version?
stages.checkpoint: Each rewrite removes the flagged risk and you can explain, specifically, why the task still works with the information that's left.

stages.title: Self-check and write the notes
stages.instructions: For each pair, write one or two sentences: what was removed, and why the rewrite doesn't lose the functionality the original had. Then run the self-check below against all three pairs before calling it done.
stages.checkpoint: All three pairs have a note that a stranger could read and understand exactly what changed and why it still works.

rubric.criterion: At least one prompt involves a real never-send category
rubric.meets: One of the three clearly involves a secret, another person's PII, or regulated data — not three mild edge cases.

rubric.criterion: The risk in each 'before' is named specifically
rubric.meets: Each before-prompt has a precise flag naming exactly what's sensitive, not a general impression.

rubric.criterion: The rewrite actually removes the risk
rubric.meets: The after-version genuinely no longer contains the flagged sensitive content — not just reworded around it.

rubric.criterion: The rewrite still does the job
rubric.meets: The after-version would still get a useful, correct result from the AI tool for the original task.

rubric.criterion: The notes explain the trade-off, not just the change
rubric.meets: Each note says why the removed detail wasn't actually needed for the task, not just that it was removed.

rubric.criterion: This reflects your actual practice, not a hypothetical exercise
rubric.meets: At least one pair is close enough to something you'd genuinely send that you could apply the same rewrite habit next time it comes up.

contentSections.body: Knowing what shouldn't be sent and being fast enough to rewrite it under real conditions are two different skills — this is the one that actually changes what you do next time.

title: Checkpoint — What Leaves Your Hands
description: Ten questions — five from this module, five pulling back to the previous one. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and the previous module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — What Leaves Your Hands

questions.from: This module — What Leaves Your Hands When You Type It
questions.prompt: When does the actual risk of a sensitive prompt occur?

options.label: The moment you hit send — nothing afterward, like deleting the message, changes it
Only if the AI's response repeats the sensitive information back
Only once the conversation is saved to your account history

questions.explanation: The request already reached the provider's servers the moment it was sent. Deleting it from the visible chat history afterward removes it from your screen, not from wherever it already arrived.

questions.from: This module — What Leaves Your Hands When You Type It
questions.prompt: Why can the same AI company have different data-handling rules for two of its own products?

options.label: Data-handling terms attach to the specific product and account tier, not the company as a whole
This never actually happens — a company's data policy is uniform across all its products
Only enterprise customers' terms are ever publicly disclosed

questions.explanation: A free consumer tier and an enterprise/API agreement from the same company commonly have different training-use defaults and retention terms — the claim has to be checked against the specific tier in use, not the brand name.

questions.from: This module — What Leaves Your Hands When You Type It
questions.prompt: What's the actual harm category when you paste someone else's PII into an AI tool, as distinct from pasting your own?

options.label: It's the same risk either way, just about a different name
It's a decision about another real person's exposure, made without their knowledge or consent
There's no meaningful difference since AI providers treat all data the same

questions.explanation: Sending your own information is a decision about your own risk tolerance. Sending someone else's identifying information is a decision you're making on their behalf, about their exposure, typically without asking them.

questions.from: This module — What Leaves Your Hands When You Type It
questions.prompt: What does a zero-data-retention (ZDR) agreement actually commit a provider to?

options.label: That the content should never have been sent to a third party in the first place
Something about what happens to data after it's transmitted and processed — like not training on it or deleting it quickly
That no human at the provider can ever access the content under any circumstance

questions.explanation: ZDR governs post-transmission handling. It says nothing about whether sending the content to a third party was the right call in the first place — that judgment still has to be made before hitting send.

questions.from: This module — What Leaves Your Hands When You Type It
questions.prompt: Why does a good personal rule need to be a small number of yes/no questions rather than a set of categories to remember?

options.label: Categories are more accurate, so they're always better if you can remember them
A rule you have to consciously look up or classify against won't survive being applied while tired or rushed, which is exactly when it's needed most
Yes/no questions are required by most AI tools' terms of service

questions.explanation: The moment you most need the rule — tired, rushed, mid-deadline — is the moment you're least likely to carefully classify something against a list of categories. A workable rule has to be fast enough to survive that moment.

questions.from: Previous module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: What does an AI model's 'default' answer actually consist of, mechanically?

options.label: The single most statistically common completion for an underspecified prompt in the training distribution
A deliberate choice made by the model's developers about what's typical
The objectively correct answer when no other detail is given

questions.explanation: It's a statistic about training text, surfaced when a prompt leaves room to guess — not a considered choice, and not evidence that the common case fits your situation.

questions.from: Previous module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: What happens to a model's confidence when it's answering about a topic thin in its training data?

options.label: It typically hedges more and sounds less certain
Its tone stays just as confident even as accuracy drops
It usually declines to answer at all

questions.explanation: Confidence doesn't track the reliability of the underlying data — which is exactly why tone can't be trusted as a signal for when to double-check an answer.

questions.from: Previous module — Whose Defaults These Are
questions.prompt: An AI-generated phone-number validator only accepts North American formats. What's the most accurate description of this?

options.label: A syntax bug that will crash on other input
A working, tested default that silently rejects real, correctly-formatted numbers from elsewhere
Not a real problem unless the product is explicitly international

questions.explanation: It compiles, validates, and ships clean — and tells users with real, correct numbers that their input is invalid, which is what makes this kind of bias easy to miss in review.

questions.from: Previous module — Whose Defaults These Are

options.label: The model ignores instructions it disagrees with
Proxies like name, address, or graduation year can carry the same information without using the literal demographic terms
The instruction only works for gender, not other categories

options.label: A step where the fix is verified against an evaluation set
A final step where the bias is confirmed gone and monitoring stops
A step where the specific failure gets documented with evidence

questions.explanation: There isn't a finish line. New failure cases keep surfacing after any fix ships, which is why ongoing monitoring is part of the process rather than an afterthought.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Where Training Data and RLHF Labeling Actually Come From
description: Two different kinds of human labor sit behind a model's output — a vast, mostly uncompensated training corpus, and a smaller, paid, often outsourced layer of human feedback. Neither is visible when you type a prompt.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish the training corpus (mostly uncompensated, scraped text) from RLHF/feedback labeling (paid, often outsourced human work)
Explain why neither form of labor is visible to someone typing a prompt

contentSections.title: Two kinds of labor, both invisible at the prompt box

contentSections.body: A novelist scrolling through an AI-generated short story recognizes a turn of phrase that's unmistakably close to their own published prose style. They never agreed to have their work used this way, and never saw a cent from it. In a different building entirely, a contract worker spends a shift reading and rating hundreds of AI outputs — some of them violent or disturbing — for a few dollars an hour, so that the model learns to produce fewer of them. Neither of these people appears anywhere in the chat window when someone types a question and gets a fluent answer back in two seconds.

There are two genuinely different kinds of human labor embedded in a deployed AI model, and it's worth keeping them separate because they raise different questions:

**The training corpus.** Large models are trained on enormous amounts of text, code, and images gathered from the public internet — books, articles, forum posts, open-source repositories, art posted online. The people who wrote or created that material mostly did not agree to have it used for this purpose, were not asked, and were not paid. Some of it is explicitly licensed in ways that at least raise questions about this use (more in the next lesson, specifically for code); a lot of it is just text someone posted, with no clear license at all, that got swept up anyway.

**RLHF and feedback labeling.** Separately, before and after a model is deployed, human reviewers rate, rank, and correct its outputs to make it more helpful and less harmful — reinforcement learning from human feedback, and its many variants. This work is paid, unlike most of the training corpus. It has also been repeatedly reported, by investigative journalists covering multiple AI companies' labeling pipelines, to be frequently outsourced to lower-wage regions, and to sometimes involve reviewing genuinely disturbing content (violence, abuse descriptions) as part of teaching a model what to refuse.

Both kinds of labor produced the fluent, instant answer in front of you. Neither is visible in the interface, and neither comes with a byline.

contentSections.scenario: Two different situations. One: a photographer's images, posted publicly on their portfolio site years ago, get scraped into a dataset used to pretrain an image model — the photographer was never contacted. Two: a worker in a data-labeling firm reviews a batch of AI-generated responses and rates each one as helpful or unhelpful, for an hourly wage.
contentSections.question: Which one is the 'RLHF/feedback labeling' layer, and which is the 'training corpus' layer?

options.label: Photographer = training corpus, worker = feedback labeling
Photographer = feedback labeling, worker = training corpus

feedback.correct: Right. The photographer's images are raw material scraped into the pretraining data — uncompensated, unconsented, and usually invisible even to the photographer unless they go looking. The worker rating outputs is doing paid, direct, after-the-fact labor specifically to shape the model's behavior.
feedback.swapped: The photographer never rated or labeled anything — their images were scraped as raw training material. The worker is the one doing direct, paid, after-the-fact labeling work on model outputs, which is the RLHF layer.

contentSections.concept: The training corpus is raw material, gathered at massive scale, mostly without consent or payment. RLHF/feedback labeling is smaller-scale, paid, direct human work shaping the model's behavior after the fact — often outsourced, and sometimes involving disturbing content. Both are labor. Neither shows up in the chat window.

contentSections.body: A fluent answer in two seconds rests on two different kinds of human labor — a vast, mostly uncompensated training corpus, and paid, often outsourced feedback labeling — and the interface shows you neither.

contentSections.title: Why 'the model learned it' doesn't erase the question

contentSections.body: "The model didn't copy your work, it learned a general pattern from millions of examples" is a real, technically accurate description of how training works in most cases. It's also not, by itself, a complete answer to whether the people whose work trained the model are owed anything — those are two different questions, and only one of them is a technical claim.

contentSections.scenario: You're evaluating arguments people make about AI training data and labor.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that is a technical claim about how models work, as opposed to a separate claim about what's owed to people.

items.label: "The model produces a general statistical pattern, not a stored copy of any one source"
"In the ordinary case, the model isn't reproducing any single training example word-for-word"
"The people whose work trained the model are owed credit or compensation"
"Because the model generalizes, no consent was needed to use the work in training"

explanation.generalizes: Technical claim — describes the mechanism of how the model actually processes training data.
explanation.no-verbatim: Technical claim — also describes the mechanism, and is generally accurate for the typical case.
explanation.owed-credit: Separate claim — this is about compensation and consent, a question the technical mechanism doesn't settle either way.
explanation.no-consent-needed: This is the muddled one — it takes a true technical claim and uses it to answer a separate question it doesn't actually answer. The mechanism being 'generalization not copying' doesn't by itself resolve whether using the work required consent.

contentSections.synthesis: Keep the two questions apart. "Does the model copy or generalize" is a technical question with a mostly-settled ordinary-case answer. "Are the people whose work trained it owed anything" is a separate, actively contested question that the technical answer doesn't resolve — treating the first as an answer to the second is where a lot of these conversations go wrong.

contentSections.body: It's worth being precise about what's actually being claimed on each side of this, because the debate gets muddled when the technical question and the labor/compensation question get treated as the same question. **The technical claim** — that a model trained on millions of examples produces a general statistical pattern rather than a stored copy of any single source — is true in the ordinary case, and it's a meaningfully different thing from plagiarism in the traditional sense of lifting a specific passage. **The separate claim** — that the people whose work made up that training data are owed consent, credit, or compensation — doesn't get resolved by the technical claim being true. This module isn't going to resolve that debate for you — it's actively contested, differently in different countries' legal systems, and still being litigated as this is being written.

"It generalizes rather than copies" is a real technical fact. It is not, by itself, an answer to whether the people whose work trained the model are owed consent, credit, or compensation — that's a separate, unresolved question.

title: Code Licensing and AI-Generated Code: What's Actually Settled and What Isn't
description: What you can say with confidence about AI-generated code and licensing, and what's still genuinely being fought out — plus the one practical check that doesn't depend on the unsettled part.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish what's legally settled about AI-generated code from what's still actively contested
Apply a practical check for near-verbatim reproduction of licensed code regardless of the unsettled legal questions

contentSections.title: Settled, unsettled, and the difference it makes

contentSections.body: An AI coding assistant, asked for a common sorting-adjacent utility function, outputs code that is close to identical to a well-known open-source library's implementation — same unusual variable names, same slightly unusual comment. That's a different, more concrete situation than the general "did training on GPL code create an obligation" debate, and it's worth knowing which situation you're actually in.

Two different questions get conflated a lot here, and only one of them has a reasonably settled answer right now:

**Unsettled:** does training a model on copyrighted or specifically-licensed code (say, GPL, which requires derivative works to carry the same license) create a licensing obligation on the model itself, or on typical output that's a *general pattern* learned from that code rather than a specific reproduction? This is genuinely contested, is the subject of active lawsuits in multiple jurisdictions as this is being written, and reasonable people — including courts — currently disagree.

**Comparatively settled:** if a specific output is a near-verbatim reproduction of a specific piece of licensed code — not a general pattern, but recognizably *that function*, with its idiosyncratic naming and structure intact — then ordinary copyright and license analysis applies to that reproduction basically the same way it would if a human developer had copy-pasted it by hand. The fact that an AI tool was the one that typed it out doesn't obviously change that a specific, identifiable copy showed up in your codebase.

The practical upshot: you don't need the big unsettled question resolved to act responsibly on the smaller, more concrete one. "Did training on open-source code in general create an obligation" is above your pay grade to resolve and not something a single developer's choices will settle. "Did this specific output look suspiciously like a specific, identifiable piece of licensed code" is a check you can actually run.

contentSections.scenario: A developer asks an AI coding assistant for a implementation of a specific, moderately unusual algorithm. The output includes a comment with the exact phrasing, including a minor typo, that appears in a well-known open-source library's public implementation of the same algorithm.
contentSections.question: What does the presence of that specific typo most plausibly indicate?

options.label: The model coincidentally generated the same typo independently — a general pattern, nothing to check further
The model's output is very likely a close reproduction of that specific source, not an independently generalized pattern — worth checking the source's license before using it

feedback.coincidence: A shared typo is a strong, specific signal — general statistical patterns don't reliably reproduce someone else's exact spelling mistake. This is much more consistent with the output being closely tied to one identifiable source.
feedback.reproduction: Right. An identical, specific typo is exactly the kind of signal that distinguishes 'the model learned a general pattern' from 'this output is closely tied to one identifiable, specific source' — which is the more settled question this lesson says you actually can check.

contentSections.mechanism: General statistical patterns don't reproduce another author's idiosyncratic mistakes. When an AI output includes something that specific and that closely matched to one known source, it's evidence you're looking at a close reproduction, not a general pattern — worth checking that source's license the same way you'd check a piece of code a human contributor submitted.

contentSections.body: The big legal question about training on licensed code in general is unsettled and above any individual developer's ability to resolve. Whether a specific output is a close reproduction of a specific, identifiable source is a check you can actually run.

contentSections.title: The check you can actually run

contentSections.body:
Treat AI-generated code you plan to ship — especially in something you'll distribute, sell, or release under a specific license — the way you'd treat a pull request from a contributor you don't know well:

1. **Watch for suspiciously specific matches** — unusual variable names, distinctive comments, an unusual structural choice that isn't just "how you'd obviously write it." Genuinely generic code (a basic loop, a standard API call) isn't a red flag; a memorable, idiosyncratic detail matching a known source is.
2. **If something looks like a specific match, search for the source.** A quick search for a distinctive string or comment often turns up the original if there is one.
3. **If you find a specific match, check that source's license** before shipping the code as-is — the same due diligence you'd apply to code copied from a Stack Overflow answer or another project, which is not a new category of problem AI introduced, just a new way to arrive at the same old one.
4. **When in doubt on genuinely unclear cases, don't treat AI-generated code as automatically license-free.** "An AI wrote it" is not a license status — it's a description of who typed it.

contentSections.question: An AI coding assistant outputs a short, completely standard for-loop with no unusual naming or structure — the kind of loop thousands of developers have independently written the same way. Does this need the same license check as the earlier typo example?
contentSections.answer: **No.** Genuinely generic code with no distinctive, identifiable fingerprint isn't a signal of reproducing one specific source — the check in this lesson is triggered by suspiciously specific matches, not by every line of AI-generated code equally.
contentSections.hint: The check is triggered by a distinctive fingerprint pointing at one specific source, not by AI involvement in general.

contentSections.body: "An AI wrote it" isn't a license status. Treat a suspiciously specific AI output the way you'd treat an unfamiliar contributor's pull request — check before you ship it.

title: When You Owe Someone Disclosure That AI Was Involved
description: Disclosure isn't one universal rule — it depends on what claim the specific context is trusting you to be making about the work.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a specific scenario for whether AI disclosure is owed, based on what claim the audience is trusting
Explain why the same amount of AI use can require disclosure in one context and none in another

contentSections.title: The question underneath the question

contentSections.body: A freelance writer uses an AI tool heavily to draft blog posts for a client, then edits them into their own voice before delivery. The client never asked, and the writer never mentioned it. Meanwhile, a different freelancer uses an AI tool lightly — just to check grammar — on a personal essay a magazine is publishing under a "in the author's own words" banner specifically because the essay's whole value is being unmediated. The second, lighter use is arguably the one with a bigger disclosure question, and the reason isn't about how much AI was involved.

The instinct to make disclosure about *how much* AI was used is understandable and it's the wrong axis. A cleaner question: **what is the audience trusting you to be claiming about this work, and does the AI use break that claim?**

- If a client is paying you for a deliverable and doesn't care how you produce it — just that it's good and on time — heavy AI use isn't breaking any claim they're relying on. This describes most freelance blog writing, most internal business writing, most code.
- If the whole point of the format is that it's unmediated — a personal essay published specifically as one person's own account, testimony, a from-the-heart letter — even light AI involvement can undercut the actual thing being sold to the reader, which is authenticity, not just competent prose.
- If there's a formal rule in place — an academic integrity policy, a journalism outlet's disclosure standard, a contest's "human-made only" rule — that rule defines the line regardless of your own judgment about whether the specific use felt like cheating.
- If someone is making a decision that depends on believing they're talking to a person specifically — a support chat where trust in a human is part of what's being relied on, a therapeutic or crisis context — disclosure isn't a courtesy, it's what lets the person calibrate how much to trust what they're being told.

contentSections.scenario: A magazine publishes personal essays under a standing editorial promise: "every essay here is the author's own words, unedited by anyone but our copyeditor for grammar." A contributor uses an AI tool to substantially restructure and rewrite their submission's arguments — more than copyediting, less than writing it from scratch — and doesn't mention this to the editor.
contentSections.question: Is disclosure owed here, and why?

options.label: No — copyediting-level help is normal and doesn't need disclosure
Yes — the magazine made a specific, explicit claim to readers about the essays being unmediated, and this use goes beyond what that claim covers

feedback.no: The magazine didn't just allow light editing — it made an explicit promise to readers about what 'unedited but for grammar' means, and substantial AI restructuring of the arguments goes well past that promise, whatever it would mean in a context with no such promise.
feedback.yes: Right. The specific, explicit claim the outlet made to its readers is what creates the disclosure obligation here — not a general rule about AI and writing, but this particular publication's particular promise, and whether this particular use breaks it.

contentSections.concept: Disclosure isn't triggered by a fixed amount of AI use — it's triggered by whether the use breaks a specific claim the audience is relying on. The same restructuring that would need no mention in an ordinary blog post breaks an explicit "unmediated" promise in this context.

contentSections.body: Ask what claim the audience is trusting you to be making, not how much AI you used. The same use can need disclosure in one context and none at all in another.

contentSections.title: The cases that actually get argued about

contentSections.body:
Two situations account for most of the genuinely hard cases, worth naming specifically:

**Formal rules that exist but weren't written with your specific use in mind.** An academic integrity policy written before AI tools existed, applied to a student who used one for brainstorming rather than drafting. A journalism outlet's AI policy written for full articles, applied to a reporter using an AI tool to transcribe an interview. The rule's letter and its spirit can genuinely diverge, and "technically not covered" is not the same as "clearly fine" — when the spirit of the rule is ambiguous for your specific use, asking the person who'd enforce it is worth the minor awkwardness of asking, compared to guessing wrong.

**Trust that depends specifically on the work being human, in a context with no formal rule at all.** A wedding toast, a condolence letter, a personal apology. Nobody is going to write a policy for these. The test from this lesson still applies: what is the recipient trusting you to be offering, and does using an AI tool to generate the actual sentiment — as opposed to using one to help organize your own already-formed thoughts — undercut that specifically? A tool helping you structure feelings you already have is different from a tool generating feelings you're presenting as your own.

contentSections.question: A student uses an AI tool only to check their already-written essay for grammar errors — no content or argument changes. Their school's integrity policy bans "submitting work not substantially your own." Is this a case where the policy's letter and spirit plausibly diverge, the way the brainstorming example was?
contentSections.answer: **No — this one's actually clear, not ambiguous.** Grammar-checking doesn't touch the argument or content at all, which is squarely outside what "not substantially your own" is aimed at. The brainstorming case was worth asking about because it was genuinely closer to the line; a pure grammar check isn't.
contentSections.hint: Compare how close this is to the actual content/reasoning of the essay, versus the brainstorming example.

contentSections.body: The hardest cases are formal rules that weren't written with your specific use in mind, and personal contexts with no formal rule at all but real trust riding on authenticity. Both still answer to the same question: what claim is being relied on, and does this use break it?

title: Passing Off AI Output as Entirely Your Own Work
description: Why the same amount of AI involvement is a non-issue in one field and a real violation in another — the line moves with what claim the field's norms actually make.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate why an identical AI-use pattern is acceptable in one professional context and a violation in another
Identify the specific claim a given field's norms make about authorship, and whether a use breaks it

contentSections.title: Same tool, different claims

contentSections.body: A developer ships production code substantially written by an AI coding assistant, reviewed and understood line by line before merging. Nobody expects a disclosure banner on the pull request — this is close to universally accepted practice, treated the same as using a compiler, an IDE's autocomplete, or a Stack Overflow answer. An artist submits AI-generated art to a competition with a plainly stated "original hand-made work only" rule, without disclosing it. These involve comparably heavy reliance on an AI tool. One is unremarkable. The other is a real violation. The difference isn't the tool.

Fields differ in what claim their norms actually make about authorship, and that's what the line tracks — not how much AI was involved:

**Software development's norm has never been "every line was typed by the author's own unaided mind."** It's always tolerated compilers, IDEs, autocomplete, copy-pasted Stack Overflow answers, and code review from colleagues, as long as the developer understands and takes responsibility for what ships. An AI coding assistant fits inside a norm that already existed; it doesn't create a new kind of authorship claim to violate.

**A hand-made-art competition's rule makes an explicit claim about process, not just outcome** — the whole premise of "original hand-made work" is that the value being judged is the human hand-skill itself, not just the final image. Using an AI tool to generate the image doesn't just skip a step; it produces a fundamentally different thing than what the category is judging, dressed up to look like the thing it isn't.

The generalizable test: **does the field's existing norm already assume tool-assisted, collaborative, or iteratively-corrected work — or does it stake its entire premise on unaided individual execution?** Software, most business writing, and most design work assume the former. Juried hand-craft competitions, academic exams designed to test unaided understanding, and personal correspondence claiming unmediated authorship assume the latter.

contentSections.code: A student argument: "My chemistry class allows using a calculator on exams, and a calculator does the arithmetic for you. An AI tool doing my exam essay's actual reasoning and writing for me is the same kind of tool use, so it should be allowed the same way."
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this argument?

options.label: Calculators and AI tools are fundamentally different kinds of technology, so the comparison never applies
The calculator is allowed because arithmetic execution isn't what the exam is testing; the essay's reasoning and writing IS what the exam is testing — so the analogy breaks exactly where it matters
AI tools weren't around when the calculator policy was written, so the policy doesn't apply to either

feedback.different-tech: The technology's nature isn't actually the deciding factor here — a calculator and a spell-checker are also different technologies, and the real test isn't about the tool's nature but what skill the assessment is trying to measure.
feedback.different-skill: Right. A calculator is allowed on a chemistry exam specifically because doing arithmetic by hand isn't the skill being tested — the reasoning about chemistry is. On an essay exam, the reasoning and writing usually ARE the skill being tested, so offloading exactly that to an AI tool undermines the test in a way that offloading arithmetic on a chemistry exam doesn't.
feedback.timing: When the policy was written doesn't determine whether the underlying logic applies — the question is whether the specific skill being offloaded is the one the assessment is actually trying to measure, which is a timeless question, not one about when a rule was drafted.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The generalizable test survives this case cleanly: ask what skill the assessment or context is actually trying to measure or claim, and whether the AI use offloads exactly that skill or something adjacent to it. A calculator offloads arithmetic on a test measuring chemistry reasoning — adjacent, not the target. An AI tool writing an essay's actual argument offloads the exact skill an essay exam exists to measure.

contentSections.body: The line isn't about how much AI was used — it's about whether the use offloads the exact thing the context is claiming to measure or value in the first place.

contentSections.title: Applying the test to your own work

contentSections.body:
For your own situation, the test from this lesson turns into a concrete question: **what is this specific piece of work claiming to demonstrate or offer, and did an AI tool produce that specific thing, or did it produce something adjacent that supports you producing the real thing yourself?**

A cover letter claims to demonstrate your own reasoning about why you fit a role — if an AI tool wrote the actual reasoning, that's the offloaded core, not an adjacent support. A cover letter where an AI tool helped you find a tighter way to phrase reasoning you'd already worked out is adjacent support, the same as a friend proofreading it. Same tool, same document type, genuinely different answer depending on which one actually happened — which is exactly why a blanket rule ("AI in cover letters: always fine" or "always not fine") misses the actual distinction that matters.

contentSections.question: Using the same test, is a novelist using an AI tool to check historical facts ("was gaslight street lighting common in this city by 1880?") while writing a historical novel offloading the core thing the novel is claiming to demonstrate?
contentSections.answer: **No.** The novel's actual claim is the author's own narrative voice, characters, and prose — fact-checking a historical detail is closer to using a reference book than to offloading the writing itself. It's adjacent support for accuracy, not a substitute for the creative work being judged.
contentSections.hint: What is a novel actually claiming to demonstrate — factual research accuracy, or narrative voice and storytelling?

contentSections.body: Ask what the piece of work is claiming to demonstrate, and whether the AI produced that specific thing or supported you producing it yourself. That answer, not a blanket rule about the format, is what settles it.

title: Writing a Disclosure That's Honest Without Being a Disclaimer Nobody Reads
description: The difference between a disclosure that actually informs someone's decision and legal boilerplate that exists to protect you, not them.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish an informative disclosure from boilerplate that primarily protects the discloser
Write a specific, honest AI-use disclosure for a real context

contentSections.title: Two disclosures, one useless

contentSections.body: "This content may have been generated in whole or in part using artificial intelligence technologies. Results may vary. Please consult a qualified professional." Somewhere on a website, in six-point gray text, nobody reads this and it changes nobody's decision. It exists to be technically true, not to inform anyone.

A disclosure has one job: **let the person receiving the work adjust how much to rely on it, and on what basis, before they rely on it.** Boilerplate fails this job even when every word in it is accurate, because accuracy isn't the same as being useful to the specific person reading it in the moment they need it.

What makes a disclosure actually work:

- **Specific, not generic.** "I used an AI tool to draft the first version of this, then rewrote the sections on X and Y myself" tells someone something. "AI may have been used" tells them nothing they can act on.
- **Placed where the decision happens**, not buried in a footer or a terms-of-service page nobody visits before reading the actual content.
- **Says what it means for reliability**, not just that a tool was involved. "I didn't independently verify the statistics in paragraph three" is a disclosure. "AI-assisted content" is a label.
- **Short.** A disclosure competing with three paragraphs of legal hedging for the reader's attention loses. One clear sentence, placed well, does more than a paragraph of protective boilerplate.

contentSections.problem: You wrote a blog post for a client using an AI tool for the first full draft, then substantially rewrote two of the four sections yourself based on your own expertise, keeping the AI's structure for the other two. The client's site has no formal AI-disclosure policy, but you've decided (using lesson three's test) that transparency here builds trust rather than undermining it. Write the disclosure.

steps.label: Identify what actually happened, specifically
steps.work: AI tool produced the first full draft; two sections were substantially rewritten based on personal expertise; two sections kept the AI-drafted structure with light editing.
steps.why: A useful disclosure has to start from an accurate, specific account of the actual process — not a rounded-off summary like 'AI helped write this.'

steps.label: Decide what a reader would actually want to know
steps.work: Which parts reflect your own judgment and expertise, and which parts are closer to the AI's own synthesis — because that's the information that changes how much weight a reader should give different parts of the piece.
steps.why: The reader's real question isn't "was AI involved, yes or no" — it's "which parts should I trust as reflecting real expertise, and which parts should I treat more skeptically."

steps.label: Write one or two sentences, specific and short
steps.work: "I used an AI tool to draft this piece, then rewrote the sections on [X] and [Y] based on my own experience — the rest kept the AI's original structure with light edits."
steps.why: This is short enough to actually get read, specific enough to be useful, and honest about exactly what a reader should weight differently.

steps.label: Place it where the decision happens
steps.work: At the top of the post, not in a footer — before the reader has invested time in content they might want to weight differently once they know the process.
steps.why: A true disclosure placed after someone has already relied on the content has already failed its one job.

faded.problem: Now a second one, same procedure. You're a freelance illustrator who used an AI image tool to generate a rough compositional sketch, then painted the final piece entirely by hand based on that sketch — no AI-generated pixels in the final image, but the composition idea came from the AI tool. You're posting the final piece publicly.

accept: used ai for composition sketch, painted by hand
blanks.why: This is a genuinely different situation from the blog post — no AI-generated content survives into the final work, only an idea for arrangement did.

blanks.prompt: What would a viewer actually want to know here — what should they weight differently?
blanks.answer: that the composition idea, not the execution, came from an AI tool
accept: the layout/composition came from ai, the painting is hand-done
blanks.why: A viewer evaluating hand-painting skill is evaluating something real and entirely the illustrator's own — the disclosure is about crediting where the compositional idea came from, a different and smaller claim than the blog example's mixed authorship.

blanks.answer: I used an AI tool to generate the initial compositional sketch for this piece; the final painting is entirely hand-done.
accept: ai generated the composition sketch, i hand-painted the final piece
blanks.why: Specific about exactly what came from where, short enough to read, and it correctly protects the actual claim being made (hand-painting skill) while being honest about the part that wasn't purely the illustrator's own idea.

contentSections.procedure: **Identify specifically what happened → decide what the audience actually needs to weight differently → write it short and specific → place it where the decision gets made.** A disclosure that skips straight to generic wording ('AI-assisted') has skipped the only two steps that make it useful.

contentSections.body: A disclosure exists to change how someone weighs the work before they rely on it. Specific and short does that. Generic and hedged, wherever it's placed, mostly protects you instead.

contentSections.title: When no disclosure is the honest answer

contentSections.body:
Worth saying plainly, because this lesson could otherwise read as "always disclose more": in contexts where AI tool use is already an unremarkable, expected part of normal practice — most code, most business writing, brainstorming, editing your own already-formed ideas — adding a disclosure doesn't inform anyone of anything they'd actually weight differently. A disclosure on every commit message noting that an AI coding assistant was used, in a team where that's standard practice for everyone, isn't transparency — it's noise that trains people to skip disclosures, including the ones that actually matter.

The same specificity test from lesson three still applies here: disclose when it changes what claim the audience should believe about the work. When it wouldn't change anything a reasonable person would do with the information, saying nothing isn't a lapse — it's a correct read of what the context actually needs.

contentSections.question: A freelancer's client explicitly asks, out of curiosity, whether AI tools were used on a project — even though the client wouldn't have cared either way if they hadn't asked. Does the 'no disclosure needed when it doesn't change anything' rule mean the freelancer can decline to answer?
contentSections.answer: **No — that rule is about proactive disclosure, not about answering a direct question honestly.** Once someone asks directly, the calculus changes: declining to answer or answering evasively is a different, worse problem than simply not volunteering the information in the first place.
contentSections.hint: The lesson's rule was about when to volunteer information unprompted — does a direct question change that?

contentSections.body: Disclosure that doesn't change what anyone would do with the information isn't extra honesty — it's noise, and noise trains people to tune out the disclosures that do matter.

description: Eight scenarios. For each, apply the 'what claim is the audience relying on' test to decide whether disclosure is owed.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the disclosure test to unfamiliar scenarios at speed
Distinguish scenarios where AI use is unremarkable from ones where it breaks a specific claim being relied on

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Eight scenarios, judged the way you'd judge your own. Nothing timed, nothing that expires.
If you kept reaching for 'it depends on how much AI was used,' go back to the actual test: what claim is being relied on, and does this use break it.

title: Lab — Write a Personal AI-Use Disclosure Policy
description: Write the policy you'd actually attach to real client or public work — specific to your own contexts, not a generic template.

learningObjectives.text: Inventory your own real AI-use contexts and the claims each one implicitly makes to its audience
Produce a written personal disclosure policy usable on real work

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: A policy you write for yourself, in advance, is a decision you make once instead of relitigating every time a deadline is close and disclosure feels like extra friction. That's the actual value of doing this now rather than case-by-case forever.

contentSections.title: Your personal AI-use disclosure policy
contentSections.brief: Write a short, real policy for your own work — the kind of thing you'd actually attach to a piece of client or public work, or keep for your own reference so you're not deciding from scratch every time.
contentSections.deliverable: A short written policy you'd actually attach to a piece of client or public work: which of your real contexts need disclosure, which don't, and the actual disclosure wording for the ones that do.

stages.title: Inventory your real contexts
stages.instructions: List 3-5 real, specific contexts where you use or might use AI tools in work you show to other people — client deliverables, published writing, code you ship, art, correspondence, anything real to your actual life. For each, name what the audience is actually relying on when they receive the work — the test from lesson three.
stages.checkpoint: You have 3-5 real contexts, each with a specific statement of what the audience is trusting about the work — not a generic list of 'writing' and 'coding.'

stages.title: Decide, context by context, where disclosure is owed
stages.instructions: For each context, apply the tests from lessons three and four: does AI use here break a specific claim the audience relies on? Is the field's norm already tool-assisted, or does it stake its premise on unaided work? Write a one-line verdict for each — disclosure owed, or not, and why.
stages.checkpoint: Every context has a specific verdict with a one-sentence reason, not just a yes/no.

stages.title: Write the actual policy
stages.instructions: Turn your verdicts into real, usable text: for each context needing disclosure, write the actual sentence or two you'd use, following lesson five's rule (specific, short, placed where the decision happens). For contexts not needing disclosure, note briefly why, so future-you doesn't have to re-derive the reasoning under deadline pressure. Then self-check the whole thing against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: Every disclosure-needed context has real, ready-to-use wording — not a placeholder — and every no-disclosure context has a one-line reason recorded.

rubric.criterion: Contexts are real, not hypothetical
rubric.meets: All 3-5 contexts are things you actually do or plausibly will do, not invented examples.

rubric.criterion: Each verdict names the specific claim at stake
rubric.meets: Every context's disclosure-or-not decision references what the audience actually relies on, not a generic 'AI feels wrong here' impression.

rubric.criterion: The disclosure wording is specific and short
rubric.meets: Each disclosure sentence says specifically what happened and what to weight differently — not generic boilerplate like 'AI-assisted content.'

rubric.criterion: It distinguishes needed from unneeded disclosure
rubric.meets: At least one context correctly concludes no disclosure is needed, with a real reason — not disclosure applied uniformly out of caution.

rubric.criterion: It's usable under pressure
rubric.meets: You could actually paste the relevant line into a real piece of work next week without rewriting it from scratch.

rubric.criterion: It reflects your own judgment, not a copied template
rubric.meets: The contexts and wording are specific to your actual work, not a generic policy that could belong to anyone.

contentSections.body: A policy decided once, in advance, is worth more than the same judgment call remade under deadline pressure every single time — that's the whole point of writing it down now.

title: Checkpoint — Whose Work This Was Built On

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve core distinctions from this module and earlier modules without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Whose Work This Was Built On

questions.from: This module — Whose Work This Was Built On
questions.prompt: What's the key difference between the 'training corpus' layer of labor and the 'RLHF/feedback labeling' layer?

options.label: The training corpus is mostly uncompensated scraped material; RLHF labeling is paid, direct human work rating and correcting outputs
They're the same thing described two different ways
The training corpus is paid; RLHF labeling is uncompensated

questions.explanation: The training corpus is raw material, gathered at massive scale, mostly without consent or payment. RLHF labeling is smaller-scale, paid, direct labor shaping model behavior after the fact.

questions.from: This module — Whose Work This Was Built On
questions.prompt: "The model generalizes rather than copies" is true in the ordinary case. What question does that technical fact NOT settle by itself?

options.label: Whether the people whose work trained the model are owed consent, credit, or compensation
Whether the model produces a stored copy of a single source
How the model processes training data mechanically

questions.from: This module — Whose Work This Was Built On

Whether a specific output is a close, identifiable reproduction of a specific licensed source
Neither question has any practical answer right now

questions.explanation: The big question about training on licensed code in general is actively contested and unsettled. Whether a specific output closely reproduces a specific identifiable source is a check you can actually run, the same as reviewing an unfamiliar contributor's code.

questions.from: This module — Whose Work This Was Built On
questions.prompt: What actually determines whether disclosure of AI use is owed in a given context?

options.label: How much of the work the AI tool produced, as a rough percentage
Whether the AI use breaks a specific claim the audience is relying on
Whether the tool used is a well-known brand name

questions.explanation: The magazine example showed a lighter AI use breaking an explicit 'unmediated' promise, while heavier use elsewhere broke no claim at all — the amount of AI use isn't what determines the disclosure obligation.

questions.from: Previous module — What Leaves Your Hands When You Type It
questions.prompt: When does the actual risk of a sensitive prompt occur?

options.label: The moment you hit send — nothing afterward, like deleting the message, changes it
Only if the AI's response repeats the sensitive information back
Only once the conversation is saved to your account history

questions.explanation: The request already reached the provider's servers the moment it was sent — deleting it afterward only removes it from your own screen.

questions.from: Previous module — What Leaves Your Hands When You Type It
questions.prompt: What does a zero-data-retention (ZDR) agreement actually commit a provider to?

options.label: That the content should never have been sent to a third party in the first place
Something about what happens to data after it's transmitted and processed — like not training on it or deleting it quickly
That no human at the provider can ever access the content under any circumstance

questions.explanation: ZDR governs post-transmission handling; it doesn't retroactively judge whether the content should have been sent anywhere in the first place.

options.label: Data-handling terms attach to the specific product and account tier, not the company as a whole
This never actually happens — a company's data policy is uniform across all its products
Only enterprise customers' terms are ever publicly disclosed

questions.explanation: A free consumer tier and an enterprise agreement from the same company commonly have different defaults — check the specific product and tier, not the brand.

options.label: Categories are more accurate, so they're always better if you can remember them
A rule that requires careful classification won't survive being applied while tired or rushed, which is exactly when it's needed most
Yes/no questions are required by most AI tools' terms of service

questions.explanation: The moment you most need the rule is the moment you're least likely to carefully classify something — a workable rule has to be fast enough to survive that moment.

A deliberate choice made by the model's developers about what's typical
The objectively correct answer when no other detail is given

The instruction only works for gender, not other categories
