title: What Actually Happens to Your Workflow When the AI Tool Goes Down
description: An outage is a free, unplanned diagnostic — it tells you, honestly, whether you were using AI to go faster at a skill you still have, or to skip a skill you no longer have.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish using AI as an accelerant on a retained skill from using it as a substitute for a skill no longer maintained
Predict which of your own tasks would stall hardest during an AI tool outage, and why

contentSections.title: The outage is a diagnostic, not just an inconvenience

contentSections.body: A developer whose daily workflow leans heavily on an AI coding assistant finds it down for six hours one afternoon. They expected to lose some speed. What actually happens is closer to a stall: several tasks that would normally take twenty minutes take most of the afternoon, not because the AI was doing something irreplaceable, but because two years of habit had quietly moved the first-draft-writing and the initial-debugging-hypothesis steps entirely onto the tool, and neither muscle had been exercised standalone in a long time.

There are two genuinely different relationships you can have with an AI tool that both look identical on a normal day and produce very different outage days:

**Accelerant on a retained skill.** You can still do the task yourself — write the function, draft the email, debug the error — and the AI tool mostly makes you faster at doing it. On an outage day, this kind of use costs you time. You're slower, back to doing it by hand, but you're not stuck.

**Substitute for a skill no longer maintained.** The AI tool isn't accelerating a skill you still have — it's doing a step you've stopped practicing, to the point that doing it unaided now takes real, effortful relearning rather than just "going slower." On an outage day, this kind of use costs you the task itself, not just speed.

The reason this distinction matters: from the outside, on a normal working day, both look exactly the same — smooth, fast, AI-assisted work. The only thing that reliably reveals which one you're actually doing is the day the tool isn't there. That's not a reason to avoid AI tools. It's a reason to occasionally, deliberately check which relationship you're actually in, on purpose, instead of finding out for the first time during an actual outage.

contentSections.scenario: During a six-hour outage, a developer finds that writing a database migration script — something they used to do routinely by hand before adopting an AI coding assistant two years ago — now takes them noticeably longer than it used to, and they have to look up syntax they used to know from memory.
contentSections.question: What does this specifically indicate about their relationship to the tool for this particular task?

options.label: The AI tool was accelerating a skill they still fully retain — this is just normal friction from an unfamiliar situation
The AI tool had become a substitute for a skill that's genuinely atrophied — the syntax and structure they used to hold in memory has quietly faded from disuse

feedback.accelerant: If the skill were fully retained, it would just take longer, not require looking things up they used to know from memory — needing to relearn syntax is a specific, concrete sign of atrophy, not just rustiness.
feedback.substitute: Right. Needing to look up syntax that used to be automatic is the tell — this isn't 'a bit slower,' it's a skill that quietly moved from 'known' to 'needs relearning' over two years of not being exercised.

contentSections.mechanism: Skills that aren't used regularly fade — this is true independent of AI, and it's exactly what happens with any tool that consistently does a step for you. The outage doesn't cause the atrophy; it reveals atrophy that was already happening quietly, one substituted instance at a time, without ever feeling like a decision to stop maintaining the skill.

contentSections.body: An outage doesn't create the problem — it reveals which of your AI-assisted tasks were speed boosts on a skill you kept, and which had quietly become the only way you knew how to do that task at all.

contentSections.title: Running your own honest inventory

contentSections.body: Most people have never actually asked themselves, task by task, which category each of their regular AI-assisted activities falls into — not because it's hard to figure out, but because a normal working day never forces the question.

contentSections.question: Someone says "I could probably figure it out" about a task they haven't done unaided in three years. Is that the same claim as "I could sit down right now and do it"?
contentSections.answer: **No — and the gap between the two is exactly where people overestimate their own readiness.** 'I could probably figure it out' usually means 'given enough time and some relearning, eventually' — which is a real but very different claim from being able to do the task right now, at normal speed and quality, unaided.
contentSections.hint: One of these claims has a hidden amount of relearning time folded into it.

contentSections.body: You don't need an actual outage to run this diagnostic — you can run it as a thought experiment, honestly, right now: pick three tasks you regularly use an AI tool for, and for each one ask **"if this tool vanished tomorrow, could I still do this task — slower, but genuinely still do it — or would I be stuck, needing to relearn something first?"** The goal isn't to feel bad about using AI tools — using them as an accelerant is exactly what a useful tool is for. It's to know, accurately, which of your dependencies are the speed-boost kind and which are the substitute kind, because the next three lessons build directly on knowing the difference.

Run the honest version of the question — 'could I do this slower, or would I be stuck relearning it' — for your own regular AI-assisted tasks. The rest of this module is about what to do with that answer.

title: Price Changes and Access Changes — Who Controls the Tool You Depend On
description: A hosted AI tool's price, availability, terms, and even whether your account stays open are all decisions someone else makes, on their timeline, not yours.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific ways a third party controls access to a hosted AI tool: pricing, deprecation, and account status
Explain why AI-tool dependency often sits deeper in a workflow than a typical SaaS dependency

contentSections.title: The lease, not the deed

contentSections.body: A small studio builds its core product — an automated first-pass editing tool for indie authors — around careful, hard-won prompt engineering against one specific AI provider's model. The provider deprecates that exact model version eighteen months later, replacing it with a newer one that behaves differently enough that the studio's carefully-tuned prompts no longer produce the same quality output. Nobody did anything wrong. The studio simply didn't own the thing its product was built on.

Using a third-party AI tool, especially a hosted API you build a product or workflow around, means depending on decisions that are entirely someone else's to make, on their timeline:

**Pricing can change**, sometimes substantially, with only as much notice as the provider's terms require — which is often not much.

**Specific model versions get deprecated** on the provider's schedule. Work carefully tuned against one version's particular behavior (a specific prompt structure, a specific quirk you learned to work around) can degrade or break when that version is retired, even if the newer version is "better" in general.

**Account access can be suspended**, sometimes by automated systems flagging a terms-of-service concern, with limited immediate human appeal — which matters more than it would for most software, because for many products the AI dependency isn't a peripheral feature, it's the thing that actually generates the core output.

This isn't unique to AI — depending on any third-party service carries some version of this risk. What's often different with AI tools specifically is how deep the dependency tends to sit: a database or a payment processor is usually swappable with real, planned effort, while an AI tool's specific behavior — the exact way it responds to your particular prompts — is often harder to replicate on a different provider even when a technically similar model is available elsewhere.

contentSections.scenario: You're assessing what's actually true about depending on a third-party AI provider for a core piece of your workflow or product.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that accurately describes real constraints of this kind of dependency.

items.label: Pricing can change with limited notice, at the provider's discretion
Specific model versions get retired on the provider's schedule, not yours
Account access can be suspended, sometimes by automated review with limited immediate appeal
Switching to a different AI provider is generally as easy as switching database vendors, since the underlying task is similar
A standard account (not a negotiated enterprise contract) usually guarantees indefinite pricing and availability

explanation.pricing: True — this is a real, documented pattern across AI providers, and standard consumer or small-business terms rarely commit to long-notice periods.
explanation.deprecation: True — models get sunset on a provider's product roadmap, and behavior tuned against one specific version's quirks doesn't automatically transfer cleanly to its replacement.
explanation.suspension: True — automated abuse-detection systems flagging an account is a real, reported failure mode, and appeal processes for smaller accounts are often slow or limited.
explanation.swap-easy: False, generally — a model's specific behavior (how it responds to your particular prompt structure, its particular quirks and strengths) is often much harder to replicate elsewhere than a database's stored data, which is exactly why AI dependency tends to sit deeper than typical SaaS dependency.
explanation.contract-guarantee: False — a standard account's terms are typically the provider's to change, and 'indefinite' guarantees are the kind of thing that specifically requires a negotiated enterprise contract, not something implied by ordinary use.

contentSections.synthesis: None of this means don't build on AI tools — it means build with the awareness that pricing, specific model behavior, and even account access are levers someone else holds, on a timeline that's theirs, not yours. That awareness is what the rest of this module turns into an actual plan.

contentSections.body: Depending on a hosted AI tool means depending on someone else's pricing decisions, someone else's deprecation schedule, and someone else's account-status judgment — all real, and all outside your control.

contentSections.title: What actually reduces this risk

contentSections.body:
This isn't a reason to avoid building on AI tools — for most people and most projects, the productivity gain is worth the dependency risk. It's a reason to take a few concrete, low-effort steps rather than being surprised later:

- **Know your actual exposure.** If a price increase or an outage happened tomorrow, would it mean an inconvenience, or would it mean your income stops? Different levels of exposure deserve different levels of preparation.
- **Avoid over-fitting to one version's specific quirks** where you reasonably can, especially for anything you're building to last — favor patterns likely to transfer if you ever need to switch providers or the version updates.
- **Read the terms of service for the specific behaviors that would actually hurt you** — rate limits, account suspension criteria, pricing-change notice periods — rather than skimming and assuming the friendly marketing tone extends to the contract terms.
- **Keep a real answer to "what would I do without this"**, which is exactly what the rest of this module is about building.

contentSections.question: A team building a product on a specific AI model version writes their prompts to work around one particular quirk of that exact version — a quirk the next version is likely to fix. Is this a wise investment of engineering effort?
contentSections.answer: **Generally not, if it can be avoided.** Over-fitting to one version's specific quirk is exactly the kind of thing that breaks when the model updates or gets deprecated — the lesson's advice to avoid over-fitting where reasonably possible is aimed precisely at this pattern.
contentSections.hint: What happens to a workaround built around a specific quirk once that quirk is fixed in the next version?

contentSections.body: You can't eliminate this dependency risk, but you can know your actual exposure, avoid over-fitting to one version's quirks, and keep a real fallback answer ready instead of discovering you need one during an actual outage.

title: Skill Atrophy: The Specific Skills That Quietly Erode
description: Not every skill erodes the same way from AI use, and the deciding factor isn't how often you use AI — it's whether you're still doing the underlying reasoning at all.

learningObjectives.text: Identify specific skills at genuine risk of atrophy from consistent AI substitution, versus ones that aren't
Explain why checking AI output after reasoning through it yourself preserves a skill that skipping the reasoning entirely does not

contentSections.title: Which skills, specifically

contentSections.body: A writer who has used an AI tool to generate every first draft for two years sits down to write something without it — not because of an outage, but because a client specifically requested "no AI, we want your own first instinct." They stare at a blank page for twenty minutes, not because they've forgotten how to write sentences, but because the specific skill of generating an initial structure from nothing — the actual hardest part of writing — hasn't been exercised in two years.

Skill atrophy from AI use isn't uniform or automatic — it's specific to which skills you've stopped exercising. Worth naming the ones that show up most often, concretely:

- **Debugging by reasoning through a stack trace yourself**, rather than pasting it and taking the first fix offered. The skill here isn't typing the fix — it's holding a hypothesis about what's actually wrong and testing it, which atrophies if you stop forming your own hypothesis before checking the AI's.
- **Generating a first draft or initial structure from a blank page** — for writing, code architecture, or a plan. This is often the actually hard part of any of those tasks, and it's exactly the part AI tools are good at doing for you, which is precisely why it's the part most likely to atrophy.
- **Basic recall and estimation** — arithmetic, syntax, facts you used to hold in working memory and now reflexively look up or generate instead. Some of this atrophy is genuinely fine (nobody mourns losing the skill of manual long division after calculators), and some of it matters more, depending on how often you need it fast and unaided.
- **Holding a multi-step plan in your head** across a longer task, instead of re-generating or re-explaining the structure to an AI tool at every step. This is a less obvious one, and arguably one of the more consequential — the ability to keep a complex plan coherent in your own head is a skill on its own, separate from whatever the plan's content is.

contentSections.scenario: You're assessing which skills genuinely atrophy from regular AI use, versus which don't meaningfully matter to lose.
contentSections.question: Select the skills that are a genuine, worth-caring-about atrophy risk from the lesson's framing.

items.label: Forming your own hypothesis about a bug before checking the AI's suggested fix
Generating an initial structure or first draft from nothing
Performing long division by hand instead of using a calculator
Holding a multi-step plan coherently in your own head across a long task
Typing speed for entering code or text manually

explanation.debug-hypothesis: Genuine risk — this is reasoning, not mechanical execution, and it's exactly the part that degrades when you consistently skip straight to the AI's answer.
explanation.blank-page: Genuine risk — generating structure from nothing is often the actual hard part of a task, and the part most consistently offloaded.
explanation.long-division: Not a meaningful loss — this was always closer to a mechanical procedure calculators are specifically good at replacing, without much reasoning content being lost.
explanation.hold-plan: Genuine, less obvious risk — the ability to keep a complex plan coherent in your own head is a distinct cognitive skill, separate from the plan's content, and it fades if a tool is always the one holding the structure.
explanation.typing-speed: Not a meaningful loss in this context — typing speed isn't the reasoning skill at stake; it's a mechanical skill unrelated to the judgment or structure-generation abilities the lesson is actually concerned with.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across the genuine risks: they're all reasoning or generative skills, not mechanical ones. Losing a mechanical shortcut (long division, manual typing speed) to a tool that does it faster isn't the same category of loss as losing the ability to form your own hypothesis or generate your own structure — the second kind is what this module is actually about protecting.

contentSections.body: Not all atrophy matters equally. Losing a mechanical shortcut to a faster tool isn't the same as losing the ability to reason through a problem or generate structure from nothing — the second kind is the one worth deliberately protecting.

contentSections.title: The habit that actually preserves the skill

contentSections.body: Two developers both use an AI assistant on every debugging session. One reads the error, forms their own hypothesis about the cause, then checks the AI's suggestion against it. The other pastes the error and takes whatever fix comes back, without forming a hypothesis first. Both look identical in their commit history. Only one of them is still exercising the skill.

contentSections.question: Of the two developers in the hook, whose skill is more likely to survive an outage or an interview whiteboard question requiring the same kind of debugging reasoning?
contentSections.answer: **The one who forms a hypothesis first.** They're still doing the actual reasoning every time, with the AI serving as a check rather than a replacement — which is exactly the skill that would need to transfer to an unaided context. The other developer has been skipping that reasoning step entirely, however identical their commit history looks.
contentSections.hint: Which developer is still exercising the actual reasoning muscle, regardless of how similar their end results look?

contentSections.body: The deciding factor for whether a skill atrophies isn't how often you use an AI tool for a task — it's **whether you're still doing the underlying reasoning yourself and using the AI to check or accelerate it, versus skipping the reasoning step entirely and going straight to the AI's answer.** This matters because it means the fix isn't "use AI less." It's a specific habit: **form your own answer first, even a rough or uncertain one, before you look at what the AI produced.** The habit is cheap. Losing the ability to reason without a tool is not — especially the day the tool isn't there, or the day you're in a context (an interview, an exam, a genuinely novel problem the AI handles badly) where that reasoning is exactly what's being asked of you.
Form your own answer first, even roughly, before checking the AI's. That single habit is most of the difference between AI keeping a skill sharp and AI quietly replacing it.

title: Deciding Which Skills You Deliberately Keep Doing by Hand
description: You can't protect every skill from every kind of atrophy, and trying to would erase most of what makes AI tools useful. A short, specific test for which ones actually deserve the effort.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a three-part test to decide which skills are worth deliberately practicing unaided
Justify a specific choice of which skills to protect, for one's own actual situation

contentSections.title: You can't protect everything, and shouldn't try to

contentSections.body: Someone reads the previous lesson and decides, with real commitment, to "do everything by hand at least sometimes" to keep every skill sharp. Two weeks later they've abandoned the whole project, because trying to protect every skill equally is exhausting, gives up most of what makes an AI tool worth using in the first place, and doesn't actually target the skills that matter most for their specific situation.

A workable answer isn't "protect everything" — it's a short, specific test for which skills earn the deliberate effort. A skill is worth keeping deliberately sharp if it passes at least one of these:

1. **It's what lets you catch the AI being wrong.** If you can no longer independently evaluate whether an AI-generated answer is actually correct — not just plausible-sounding — you've lost your ability to supervise the tool, which is a different and more serious loss than losing raw speed.
2. **It's needed in a context where the AI genuinely won't be there.** An interview, a licensing exam, a client meeting where you're asked to reason out loud in real time, a context where using the tool isn't allowed or isn't available. If a skill only ever gets exercised with AI assistance and a real situation exists where you won't have that assistance, that's a concrete, not hypothetical, reason to protect it.
3. **It's the specific thing you're actually paid or valued for.** A skill that's the professional core of what makes your work yours — the judgment, not the typing — is worth protecting even if an AI tool could technically do a passable version of it, because losing it changes what you're actually offering, not just how fast you offer it.

A skill that fails all three — nice to have, never load-bearing for catching errors, never needed unaided, and not core to your professional value — is a completely reasonable one to hand off entirely and stop worrying about.

contentSections.code: A senior developer's reasoning: "I'll deliberately keep my CSS flexbox syntax sharp by writing it unaided sometimes, since I use AI for it constantly. I won't bother keeping my code-review judgment sharp — I use AI to help review PRs too, and reviewing is basically the same kind of task."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this developer's prioritization, using the three-part test?

options.label: CSS syntax and code-review judgment are both equally low-priority — neither is worth protecting

The developer has it backwards — code-review judgment is exactly the skill that catches AI being wrong and is core to their professional value, while flexbox syntax is closer to a mechanical detail that fails all three tests

feedback.both-low: Code-review judgment is precisely the kind of skill the test flags as high-priority — it's what catches an AI-generated (or anyone else's) mistake before it ships, and it's a core part of what makes a senior developer's judgment valuable.
feedback.backwards: Right. Flexbox syntax is a lookup-able mechanical detail that fails all three tests — losing quick recall of it doesn't stop you from catching errors, isn't needed in most no-AI contexts, and isn't the core of a senior developer's value. Code-review judgment is exactly the opposite: it's what lets you catch the AI being wrong, and it's closer to the actual professional core of the job.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This is a common, understandable mistake: protecting the skill that feels most 'technical' and visible (syntax) while neglecting the one that's actually load-bearing (judgment) because judgment doesn't feel like a skill you 'practice' the same concrete way. The three-part test exists specifically to redirect effort toward what actually matters instead of what's easiest to notice.

contentSections.body: Protect a skill if it lets you catch the AI being wrong, if you'll genuinely need it unaided somewhere, or if it's the actual core of what you're valued for. Everything else is a reasonable thing to hand off without guilt.

contentSections.title: Applying it to your own list

contentSections.body:
Run the three-part test against your own regular AI-assisted tasks, honestly, and you'll usually end up with a short list — most people land on somewhere between two and four skills that genuinely pass at least one criterion, out of a much longer list of things AI helps with day to day. That's the intended outcome, not a failure of the exercise: the test is designed to be selective, because a list of twenty "skills to protect" is exactly as unsustainable as the all-or-nothing approach from the start of this lesson.

The next lesson turns this list into an actual concrete plan — not just a list of good intentions, but specific steps for the day you'd actually need one of these skills without the tool.

contentSections.question: Someone's list of "skills to protect" has eight items on it after running the three-part test. What does that suggest?
contentSections.answer: **Probably that the test is being applied too generously.** The test is meant to be selective — most people land on two to four genuine passes. Eight items suggests some of them are being included for 'nice to have' reasons rather than actually passing one of the three specific criteria.
contentSections.hint: Compare this to the lesson's stated realistic target range.

contentSections.body: A short, honestly-prioritized list beats a long, well-intentioned one you'll abandon in two weeks. Two to four skills, chosen by the test, is a realistic target.

title: A Concrete Fallback Plan for a Day the Tool Isn't Available
description: The difference between a real fallback plan and a good intention is whether it's specific enough to actually follow at 9am on the day you need it, and whether it's ever been tested before that day.

learningObjectives.text: Write a specific, actionable outage contingency plan naming which tasks wait and which need a hand-done path
Explain why an untested fallback plan is unreliable in a way a tested one isn't

contentSections.title: A plan you've never run isn't tested

contentSections.body: Someone writes, with genuine good intentions, "if the AI tool is ever down, I'll just do things manually." It's not wrong, exactly — it's just not actually a plan. It doesn't say which tasks, which ones can wait a day, or whether the person could actually still do the manual version fast enough to matter. It's the fire-safety-plan equivalent of "I'll just get out of the building."

A plan that actually holds up under pressure needs three specific things a vague intention doesn't have:

1. **A task-by-task triage**, not a blanket statement. Some tasks genuinely can wait a few hours or a day for the tool to come back — no plan needed beyond patience. Others can't, and those are the ones that need an actual named alternative.
2. **A named alternative for each urgent task** — not "I'll figure it out," but the actual specific action: which reference you'd check, which colleague you'd ask, which slower manual process you'd follow, and roughly how long it would actually take.
3. **Periodic testing**, not a document written once and never touched. The skills lesson four flagged as worth protecting need occasional real practice, unaided, on purpose — a fire drill, not a fire escape map nobody's ever walked. A skill that was fine two years ago when the plan was written may have quietly atrophied exactly the way lesson three described, and the only way to know is to actually try it occasionally, not assume the plan is still accurate.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in a sensible order for building a real fallback plan, not just a document of good intentions.
steps: List the specific tasks you regularly depend on an AI tool for
For each, decide honestly whether it could wait for the tool to return, or needs an immediate alternative
For the ones that can't wait, name the specific alternative action and how long it would realistically take
Periodically test the plan by actually doing one of the tasks unaided, on purpose
contentSections.explanation: Skipping the honest triage step and going straight to alternatives wastes effort naming fallbacks for tasks that could have just waited. Skipping the testing step is how a plan quietly goes stale — the alternative you wrote down two years ago assumed a skill level you may no longer have, and the only way to catch that is to actually try it before the day you're relying on it for real.

contentSections.body: A real fallback plan triages task by task, names specific alternatives (not 'I'll figure it out'), and gets periodically tested — not written once and trusted forever.

contentSections.title: Writing one for real

contentSections.body:
Here's a worked, compressed example, for a freelance developer who relies heavily on an AI coding assistant:

> **Can wait a day:** Generating boilerplate for new features, drafting documentation, exploratory refactoring ideas. No urgent alternative needed — these can simply wait for the tool to return.
>
> **Can't wait — needs a named alternative:** Debugging a production incident. Alternative: work through the stack trace manually using the same task→access-method→where-it-stops reasoning process I already know from experience, check the team's runbook for common past incidents, ping the on-call colleague if it's genuinely stuck after 30 minutes. Realistic time: 2-3x longer than AI-assisted, but functional.
>
> **Test:** Once a month, deliberately debug one real issue without AI assistance, timed, to confirm the 2-3x estimate still holds and the skill hasn't quietly slipped further than that.

Notice this plan doesn't try to cover everything — it covers the handful of tasks that actually matter, with real specifics attached to each, and a built-in way to notice if the plan has gone stale. That's a genuinely different document than "I'll manage."

contentSections.question: In the worked example, why does the plan include a monthly timed test rather than just trusting the '2-3x longer' estimate once it's written down?
contentSections.answer: **Because the estimate itself can go stale.** The skill it's based on can keep atrophying quietly (as lesson three described) even after the plan is written — the monthly test is what actually catches that drift, instead of discovering the estimate was wrong on the day of a real incident.
contentSections.hint: What could change about the underlying skill between when the plan is written and when it's actually needed?

contentSections.body: A good fallback plan is short, specific to the tasks that actually can't wait, and includes its own test — not a promise to yourself you'll never actually check.

title: Lab — Write Your Own AI-Outage Contingency Plan

Produce a specific, testable outage contingency plan naming the skills deliberately kept sharp

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the module's actual deliverable — everything from the honest inventory in lesson one through the three-part skill test in lesson four turns into one real, usable document by the end of this lab.

contentSections.title: Your AI-outage contingency plan
contentSections.brief: Write the plan you'd actually want in hand the day your primary AI tool becomes unavailable — whether from an outage, a price change that puts it out of reach, or an account issue. This should reflect your real workflow, not a hypothetical one.
contentSections.deliverable: A written plan naming the 2-3 skills you keep sharp by hand and what you'd do the day access disappears — specific enough to actually follow, not a general statement of intent.

stages.instructions: List the tasks you regularly use an AI tool for. For each, run the lesson-one diagnostic honestly: accelerant on a retained skill, or substitute for one that's atrophied? Then run the lesson-four three-part test on each to identify candidates worth deliberately protecting.

For the ones that can't wait, name the actual specific alternative action — not 'I'll figure it out' — and a realistic honest estimate of how much longer it would take.

stages.title: Write the plan and its own test
stages.instructions: Assemble the inventory, the triage, and the alternatives into one short, usable document. Add a specific, scheduled way you'll periodically test it — an actual practice you'll do, not just a promise to check in someday. Then self-check against the rubric below.

rubric.criterion: It reflects your real workflow

rubric.criterion: The atrophy assessment is honest

rubric.criterion: It includes a real, scheduled test
rubric.meets: Names a specific, recurring practice for checking the plan still holds — not just a one-time document.

rubric.criterion: It's short enough to actually use
rubric.meets: You could reread the whole thing in under two minutes on the day you actually needed it.

contentSections.body: The value of this plan isn't in having written it once — it's in the specific alternatives being real enough, and tested enough, to actually work on the day you need them.

title: Why a Rule You Can't Apply Under Deadline Pressure Isn't a Real Rule
description: Everything from this phase — bias-checking, privacy discipline, disclosure judgment, dependence-awareness — has to survive a bad, rushed day, not just a calm reading day, or it isn't actually a rule you have.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why deliberate, careful reasoning tends to be the first thing skipped under time pressure
Evaluate whether a personal rule from this phase is actually fast enough to survive real deadline pressure

contentSections.title: Good intentions have a failure mode, and it's predictable

contentSections.body: A freelancer who genuinely internalized every principle from this phase — checked defaults for bias, was careful about what went in a prompt, thought hard about disclosure, kept a couple of skills sharp by hand — has a client emergency at 4:45pm on a Friday. By 5:10pm, none of that is happening. Not because the principles stopped being true. Because careful, deliberate reasoning is expensive, and the moment that expense feels unaffordable is exactly the moment good intentions quietly get skipped.

This isn't a character flaw specific to any one person — it's a predictable, well-documented pattern: **time pressure and cognitive load systematically favor fast, habitual responses over slow, deliberate ones**, and everything this phase has taught — checking a default for bias, deciding what's safe to paste, weighing whether disclosure is owed, noticing dependence — is a slow, deliberate kind of reasoning by nature. That's not a flaw in the reasoning. It just means a version of these principles that only exists as "things I know and would apply if I had time to think" will reliably not survive contact with an actual deadline.

The entire point of the last four modules turning into short, fast rules — a three-question privacy check, a specific disclosure test, a two-to-four-item list of protected skills — was to compress genuinely careful reasoning into something fast enough to survive exactly this moment. If your version of any of them still takes real, unhurried thought to apply, it isn't finished yet.

contentSections.scenario: A developer who normally reviews AI-generated code carefully for the kind of assumed defaults covered earlier in this phase ships a form validator without that review, during a release crunch, and it turns out to have the same US-only assumption problem from module one.
contentSections.question: What's the most accurate explanation for why the review got skipped?

options.label: The developer decided, in that moment, that bias-checking wasn't important enough to bother with
Time pressure crowded out the slower, deliberate review step, defaulting to the faster habitual action (shipping the code) instead

feedback.decided: There's no evidence of an actual decision happening — nothing in the scenario suggests the developer weighed the review and consciously chose to skip it. That's exactly the point: it wasn't a decision, it was the review simply not happening under load.
feedback.crowded-out: Right. Under real time pressure, the slower, deliberate step is what gets crowded out — not because anyone judged it unimportant, but because it's the more expensive kind of cognition, and expensive things get skipped first when the budget runs short.

contentSections.mechanism: Deliberate reasoning has a real cognitive cost, and that cost becomes the first thing dropped under load — not through a conscious decision to deprioritize it, but simply by being the more expensive option in a moment where the cheap, habitual option is available. A rule that only works as deliberate reasoning is a rule that predictably won't survive this exact, common moment.

contentSections.body: Deliberate reasoning is the first thing time pressure crowds out — not from a conscious choice to skip it, but because it's the expensive option. A rule that only works with unhurried thought isn't a rule you actually have.

contentSections.title: Testing your own rules against this

contentSections.body: This phase asked you to write several fast rules along the way — a privacy check, a disclosure test, a short list of protected skills. It's worth actually testing whether they pass the standard this lesson just set, rather than assuming they do because you wrote them thoughtfully.

contentSections.question: You wrote a privacy rule that's three specific yes/no questions, each answerable by looking at the content in front of you. Does this pass the deadline-pressure test from this lesson?
contentSections.answer: **Yes, on its face — that's exactly the shape that survives pressure.** Short, specific, answerable from the content itself rather than requiring lookup or extended thought. The real test isn't just the shape, though — it's whether you'd actually run it at 4:45pm on a Friday, which is a habit question, not just a design question.
contentSections.hint: Compare this shape to the failure case from this lesson's hook — what made that developer's review skip happen?

contentSections.body: A rule passes this test if it's **short enough to run in seconds, specific enough that you don't have to think hard about how to apply it, and phrased as a check against the actual thing in front of you rather than an abstract principle to remember.** If any rule you've written across this phase requires you to recall a longer explanation, weigh multiple factors carefully, or look something up, it's still in the "good intention" stage, not the "actual rule" stage — and this module's job is closing that gap, one real decision at a time.
A rule survives deadline pressure if it's fast, specific, and checkable against what's actually in front of you. If it needs unhurried thought, it isn't finished — that's the gap this module closes.

title: Weighing Competing Concerns When They Conflict
description: Speed, privacy, disclosure, and bias don't always point the same direction. A framework for making the call when they genuinely pull against each other, instead of just picking whichever concern you noticed first.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when multiple concerns from this phase genuinely conflict in a real scenario
Apply an irreversibility-first heuristic to prioritize between conflicting concerns

contentSections.title: The decisions that actually feel hard

contentSections.body: A journalist on a tight deadline has a leaked internal document containing both the story's key facts and several named private individuals' contact information. Summarizing it with an AI tool would be fast. The document is also large enough that the fastest path risks pasting more of it than needed, the outlet's AI disclosure policy doesn't clearly address source-document handling, and skimming it manually first would blow the deadline. Every concern from this phase is present in one decision, and they don't agree with each other.

Most of this phase's earlier scenarios isolated one concern at a time, because that's how you learn to recognize each one. Real decisions rarely arrive isolated — speed pressure, privacy risk, disclosure ambiguity, and bias risk show up together and pull in different directions, and "just weigh them all carefully" isn't actually a method, it's a description of the problem.

A workable method needs an actual tiebreaker, not just a longer list of things to consider. The one that holds up across most real cases: **ask which concern, if violated, causes harm that can't be undone — and resolve that one first, even if it costs you on the others.**

- A **privacy leak** of a real, identifiable person's information, once sent, can't be unsent — this is irreversible in exactly the way lesson one of module two established.
- A **bias-affected output** can usually be caught and corrected in review before it reaches anyone, if you're looking for it — reversible, if you check.
- A **disclosure gap** can often, though not always, be corrected after the fact — a late but honest disclosure is imperfect but usually better than none, which makes it a real-but-lesser harm compared to a leak that can never be walked back.
- **Missing a speed goal** is real and can have serious consequences of its own, but it's the one most likely to be recoverable — a late deliverable is a bad outcome, not usually an unrecoverable one.

contentSections.scenario: In the hook's scenario, the journalist has to choose between: (a) redacting the private individuals' details before using an AI tool to summarize, which takes 20 extra minutes they don't have, or (b) summarizing the full document as-is to hit the deadline, planning to remove any private details from the published story afterward.
contentSections.question: Using the irreversibility-first heuristic, which is the more defensible call?

options.label: Option (b) — hit the deadline, since the private details won't appear in the final published story either way
Option (a) — the 20-minute redaction, because the leak risk from the AI tool exposure itself happens the moment it's sent, regardless of what makes it into the final published piece

feedback.b: This confuses two different exposure points. Removing private details from the *published story* doesn't undo the fact that those details were already sent to a third-party AI tool — the privacy exposure this heuristic cares about happens at the moment of transmission, not at publication.
feedback.a: Right. The privacy exposure is irreversible the moment the document is sent, regardless of later editorial decisions. Missing the deadline by 20 minutes is a real cost, but it's the recoverable one — the leak isn't.

contentSections.concept: The irreversibility-first heuristic: when concerns conflict, resolve the one that can't be undone before the ones that can, even at real cost to the others. A missed deadline can usually be explained and absorbed. A privacy leak, once sent, cannot.

contentSections.body: When concerns genuinely conflict, resolve the irreversible one first — usually privacy — even at real cost to speed. Bias is often catchable in review; disclosure is often fixable after the fact; a leak is not.

contentSections.title: When it isn't privacy that's irreversible

contentSections.body: The heuristic isn't "privacy always wins" — it's "irreversibility wins," and privacy just happens to be the most commonly irreversible concern in these scenarios. It's worth having a case where a different concern is actually the irreversible one.

contentSections.question: A company is about to publicly launch a customer-facing AI feature that, in testing, showed a bias pattern against a specific demographic that hasn't yet been fixed — but launch has already been publicly announced for tomorrow, and delaying costs real reputational and financial harm. Using the irreversibility-first heuristic, what's the right read?
contentSections.answer: **The bias harm here is the irreversible one, not the delay.** Once real users start receiving biased output in production, that harm has already landed on real people and can't be undone — whereas the cost of delaying a launch, while real and painful, is a recoverable business cost. This flips the usual pattern precisely because the bias issue here is about to become irreversible in the way privacy leaks usually are.
contentSections.hint: Ask which harm, once it happens, can't be walked back — the delay's cost, or the effect on the first real users who get the biased output?

contentSections.body: This is the actual generalizable version of the heuristic: it's not a ranked list where privacy always beats bias which always beats disclosure which always beats speed. It's a question you ask fresh each time — **which concern, in this specific situation, is the one that can't be undone once it happens** — and that can be any of the four, depending on the specifics. The four-concern list from this phase gives you the vocabulary to notice what's in tension. The irreversibility question is what actually breaks the tie.

The heuristic isn't a fixed ranking of concerns — it's a live question asked fresh each time: which harm, once it happens, can't be walked back? That's the one to resolve first, whichever concern it turns out to be.

title: A Case Where 'Don't Use AI for This' Was the Right Call
description: Not a general anti-AI stance — a specific decision that holds up because of what the stakes and claims actually were in that particular case.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate why declining to use an AI tool was the right call in a specific case, based on stakes and claims rather than general caution
Distinguish a defensible case-specific 'no' from a general anti-AI stance

contentSections.title: The case

contentSections.body: A small mental-health support line, stretched thin and genuinely considering a well-reviewed AI chatbot to triage incoming messages after hours, decides not to deploy it — despite real capacity strain and a tool that tested reasonably well on typical queries. Six months later, a comparable organization's deployment mishandles a message from someone in acute crisis, missing urgency signals a trained human volunteer would have caught. The first organization's 'no' wasn't caution for its own sake. It was a specific, defensible read of what was actually at stake.

Walking through why this specific 'no' holds up, using this phase's own vocabulary:

**The claim being relied on (module three's framing):** someone reaching out in crisis is relying on being heard by something that can recognize the full weight and specific texture of what they're saying — not just pattern-match against typical phrasing. An AI tool that's fluent on ordinary queries can still miss the specific, sometimes indirect way acute crisis actually presents, and a wrong read here isn't a quality-of-service problem, it's a safety problem.

**The irreversibility (this module's lesson two):** a missed or mishandled crisis signal is about as irreversible a harm as exists in this whole framework — there's no correcting it after the fact the way you could revise a biased blog draft or issue a late disclosure.

**The dependence risk (module four):** if the organization built its after-hours capacity entirely around the tool, an outage or a subtle failure mode wouldn't just be an inconvenience — it would be a capability gap at exactly the moment it's most needed, with no tested fallback.

Stacking those together — a severe, hard-to-catch, irreversible risk, in a domain where the trust claim is specifically about being understood by something that gets the stakes — produces a 'no' that isn't general skepticism of AI tools. It's the same framework this whole phase built, applied honestly to a case where every factor pointed the same direction.

contentSections.scenario: Someone hears about this organization's decision and concludes: "So this proves AI tools are too risky for any healthcare-adjacent use."
contentSections.question: Is that the right lesson to draw from this specific case?

options.label: Yes — if it's not safe here, it's not safe in any healthcare-adjacent context
No — this was a specific call based on this situation's particular stakes, claim, and irreversibility, not a general verdict on AI in healthcare-adjacent work

feedback.generalize: This overreaches past what the case actually showed. The specific combination here — acute crisis detection, severe and irreversible failure mode, a trust claim about being understood — doesn't automatically transfer to, say, an AI tool that helps a clinic schedule routine appointments, where the stakes and claims are entirely different.
feedback.specific: Right. This was a case-specific call, built from the actual stakes, claim, and irreversibility of this particular use — not a general rule about an entire industry. A different healthcare-adjacent use with lower stakes and a different trust claim could reasonably land on a different answer.

contentSections.concept: A well-reasoned case-specific 'no' resists generalizing past the specific factors that produced it. The value of walking through why this call was right is in the method — stakes, claim, irreversibility — not in exporting the verdict wholesale to every superficially similar situation.

contentSections.body: A defensible 'don't use AI here' is built from this specific situation's stakes, claim, and irreversibility — not a general verdict that gets exported to every similar-sounding case.

contentSections.title: What made this a genuinely hard call, not an obvious one

contentSections.body: It's worth being honest that this wasn't a free decision — the organization was genuinely stretched thin, and 'no AI tool' meant real, ongoing strain on already-limited human capacity. A framework that only works on easy cases where there's no real cost to the safer choice isn't actually being tested.

contentSections.question: Does the fact that declining the tool cost the organization something real (ongoing capacity strain) make the decision less defensible?
contentSections.answer: **No — if anything, it's what makes the decision meaningful rather than free.** A framework that only produces the cautious answer when caution is costless isn't actually doing any work. The fact that this organization paid a real cost for the safer call, and the reasoning still held up, is exactly what makes it a strong example rather than an easy one.
contentSections.hint: A decision with no real trade-off attached isn't much of a test of the reasoning behind it.

contentSections.body: This is worth sitting with, because it's the honest version of what applying this phase's framework actually costs sometimes: the right call, by this reasoning, was also the harder and more expensive one to make in the moment. That's not a flaw in the framework — a decision framework that only ever recommends the easy, free option isn't actually adjudicating anything. What makes this case worth studying is that the stakes-claim-irreversibility reasoning held up even when the safer answer wasn't the convenient one, which is the actual test of whether a piece of reasoning is real or just a justification for whatever was going to happen anyway.
The decision cost something real, and the reasoning held up anyway — that's what makes it a genuine test of the framework, not an easy call dressed up as a hard one.

title: A Case Where Heavy AI Use Was the Right Call
description: The same framework, applied honestly to a case where nearly every factor points the other way — not 'AI is fine here' by default, but by the actual math coming out low-risk.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate why heavy AI use was defensible in a specific case, using the same stakes/claim/irreversibility framework as the opposite case
Apply the phase's framework symmetrically, rather than treating caution as always the safe default answer

contentSections.title: The case

contentSections.body: A small internal tools team builds an AI-assisted script that auto-generates draft release notes from commit messages and PR descriptions, for an internal engineering wiki nobody outside the company sees. It's heavily AI-generated, lightly reviewed, and shipped fast. Using the exact same framework from the previous lesson, this is a genuinely easy 'yes' — worth walking through precisely because it's the same reasoning, not a different, more permissive one.

Running the same stakes-claim-irreversibility check from lesson three, honestly, on this case:

**The claim being relied on:** nobody reading internal release notes is relying on a claim of unmediated human authorship — the norm here, per module three, already assumes tool-assisted, lightly-reviewed internal documentation. There's no claim being broken.

**The irreversibility:** a wrong or oddly-phrased release note is easy to notice and easy to fix — someone edits the wiki page. This is about as reversible a failure mode as exists in this whole framework.

**The dependence risk:** if the tool goes down, someone writes release notes manually, the way every team did before AI drafting tools existed — a minor inconvenience, not a capability gap with real stakes attached, because this was never load-bearing infrastructure.

**The bias and privacy exposure:** commit messages and PR descriptions are internal, already-written by the team's own engineers, not third-party PII or regulated data — and release-note phrasing carries essentially no consequential bias risk the way a hiring recommendation would.

Every factor that made the crisis-line case a hard 'no' comes out low here. That's not a coincidence and it's not special pleading for this particular case — it's the same framework, run honestly, landing somewhere else because the actual situation is different.

contentSections.code: A team lead's reasoning: "We already decided AI tools carry real risk in module two through four of this phase, so as a rule, we should minimize AI use across the board to stay safe, including for internal tooling like this."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this reasoning?

options.label: It correctly applies a general caution principle consistently
It treats 'minimize AI use' as the safe default in every case, when the actual framework says to run the specific factors each time — and this case's factors come out low-risk across the board

feedback.correct: This isn't actually applying the framework — it's replacing it with a blanket rule the framework never recommended. The whole point of the stakes-claim-irreversibility check is that it can come out either way depending on the actual case.
feedback.flaw: Right. Treating caution as the universal safe default undoes the actual value of the framework, which is specifically that it distinguishes cases — a hiring tool and an internal release-notes generator don't carry the same risk just because they're both 'AI use,' and pretending they do produces worse decisions, not more careful ones.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A framework that always lands on 'be more cautious' regardless of the actual stakes isn't a framework — it's a mood. The value of running stakes, claim, and irreversibility explicitly, every time, is that it sometimes produces 'go ahead, this is fine,' and a team lead who skips that possibility is doing less analysis than the framework asks for, not more.

contentSections.body: Run honestly, the same framework that produced a hard 'no' in the crisis-line case produces an easy 'yes' here — because the actual claim, irreversibility, and risk factors are genuinely different, not because the framework relaxed.

contentSections.title: Why this case is worth taking seriously too

contentSections.body: It would be easy to read this lesson as the throwaway 'and here's a boring low-stakes example, moving on.' It's worth taking seriously for a specific reason: this is what most real AI-use decisions actually look like, and a framework that only gets exercised on dramatic edge cases isn't the one you'll actually reach for on an ordinary Tuesday.

contentSections.question: Which case — the crisis-line 'no' or the release-notes 'yes' — is a more realistic template for the decisions you'll actually face most often?
contentSections.answer: **For most people, the release-notes case, by a wide margin.** Dramatic, high-stakes, obviously-hard calls are rare. The genuinely useful skill from this phase is running the same honest check on the ordinary, low-drama decisions that make up most of a real week — and noticing, correctly, when the answer is just 'yes, this is fine.'
contentSections.hint: Think about how often you actually face a genuinely high-stakes AI-use decision, versus an ordinary one.

contentSections.body: The skill this phase is actually building isn't "know when to refuse AI tools" — it's **being able to run the same honest check quickly enough to use on ordinary decisions, and trust the answer whichever way it comes out.** A framework you only trust when it produces caution isn't a framework, it's a bias with extra steps. Trusting it when it says "this is genuinely fine, go ahead" is just as much the point as trusting it when it says stop.

Most real decisions look more like the release-notes case than the crisis-line case. The actual skill is running the same honest check quickly on ordinary decisions and trusting whichever answer it gives.

title: Writing Your Own Working Rules Down Where You'll Actually See Them Again
description: A rule in a document you never reopen isn't a rule you have — it needs to live where the actual decision happens, not in a file you wrote once and forgot.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a rule's storage location matters as much as its content for whether it's actually used
Embed a personal working rule into an actual point of decision in one's own workflow

contentSections.title: Where a rule lives determines whether it exists

contentSections.body: Someone finishes this entire phase, writes a thoughtful, genuinely good set of personal rules — privacy check, disclosure test, protected-skills list, the irreversibility heuristic — into a document, saves it, and never opens that document again. Six months later, none of it is influencing a single actual decision. The rules were good. Their storage location made them irrelevant.

A rule that lives in a document you have to remember to reopen is competing against every other thing pulling at your attention in the actual moment of decision, and it reliably loses that competition — not because the rule is bad, but because "go check the document" is itself an extra deliberate step, and lesson one of this module already established what happens to deliberate steps under real conditions.

The fix isn't a better document. It's **placing the rule inside something you're already going to touch at the exact moment the decision happens** — not adjacent to your workflow, inside it:

- A privacy check embedded as the first line of your own prompt-writing template, so you see it every time you open a new AI chat for real work, not in a separate file about privacy.
- A disclosure reminder built into the template you already use for client deliverables, not a policy page you'd have to think to visit.
- Your protected-skills list as a recurring calendar reminder tied to an already-existing habit (a monthly retro, a standing 1:1), not a note in an app you don't open on your own.

The test for whether a rule is actually placed well: **would you encounter it even on a day you weren't thinking about ethics at all** — because that's every ordinary working day, and that's exactly when it needs to be there.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in order for turning a good rule into one that actually gets used.
steps: Write the rule itself, short and specific
Identify the exact moment and tool where the relevant decision actually happens
Place the rule inside that existing moment, not in a separate document
Check, after a week of normal work, whether you actually encountered it without having to remember to look
contentSections.explanation: Skipping the placement step and stopping at 'I wrote it down somewhere' is the single most common way a genuinely good rule from this phase quietly stops mattering. The final check — did you actually encounter it without remembering to look — is what tells you honestly whether the placement worked.

contentSections.body: A rule's storage location is not a detail — it's the difference between a rule you actually have and a document you wrote once. Place it inside a moment you're already going to be in, not beside it.

contentSections.title: This phase, compressed to what you'll actually carry forward

contentSections.body: Five modules, twenty lessons, and a lot of specific scenarios later, it's worth being honest about what actually survives into ordinary practice — not everything covered gets carried forward with equal weight, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of unrealistic rule.

contentSections.question: If you could keep only three things from this entire phase in active, working memory — not a document, but things you'd actually reach for — which kind of thing would be most valuable to keep: specific facts (like exact retention-window numbers), or short, fast tests (like the three-question privacy check)?
contentSections.answer: **The short, fast tests, by a wide margin.** Specific facts (a provider's exact current policy, a particular legal detail) go stale and need re-checking anyway. The tests — the privacy check, the disclosure test, the irreversibility heuristic, the stakes-and-claim question — are what's actually reusable indefinitely, on any new situation this phase never specifically covered.
contentSections.hint: Which kind of thing stays true and useful longer: a specific current fact, or a method for reasoning through a new case?

contentSections.body: That's the actual design of this phase, made explicit at the end: the specific scenarios were vehicles for building a small number of fast, reusable tests, not a catalog of cases to memorize. New situations this phase never mentioned will come up — a tool that didn't exist yet, a context none of these lessons described — and the thing that transfers to them isn't a memorized answer, it's the handful of short questions you can run on anything: what claim is being relied on, what's irreversible here, could I actually explain this decision to someone who disagreed with it. That's what this module's lab asks you to do for real, on a decision that's actually yours.
What actually transfers from this phase isn't the specific scenarios — it's a small number of fast, reusable tests you can run on a situation none of these lessons ever described.

title: Practice — Apply Your Rules to Seven Ambiguous New Scenarios
description: Seven scenarios spanning bias, privacy, disclosure, and dependence — none of them exactly like the module's worked examples. Apply the phase's actual tests, not memorized answers.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the phase's reusable tests (claim, irreversibility, stakes) to genuinely new scenarios
Justify a call on an ambiguous scenario using the phase's framework rather than intuition alone

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven new scenarios, none identical to the module's worked examples on purpose — that's the actual test of whether the reasoning transfers. Nothing here is timed.
If you found yourself reaching for a memorized answer instead of running the actual test, that's worth noticing — the test is what's supposed to transfer, not any specific case.

title: Lab — Write Your AI-Use Decision Memo
description: Take one real, current decision you're actually facing and write out the call, with reasoning, you'd defend to someone who disagreed with you.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the phase's full framework to one real, current, personally-relevant decision
Produce a written decision memo defensible to a specific, informed skeptic

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the phase's actual capstone move: not a hypothetical case study, but a real decision you're genuinely facing, reasoned through with everything from bias-checking through dependence-planning, and written up well enough to survive someone pushing back on it.

contentSections.title: Your AI-use decision memo
contentSections.brief: Pick one real, current, or recently-faced decision involving AI use in your actual work or life — not a hypothetical. It should be genuinely ambiguous to you, not one where the answer is obvious. Write the memo you'd actually want in hand if someone who disagreed with your call pushed back on it.
contentSections.deliverable: A written decision memo: the decision, the reasoning, and the rule it came from — specific enough to defend to a real, informed skeptic.

stages.title: State the decision and the competing concerns honestly
stages.instructions: Name the actual decision in one sentence. Then, using this phase's four concerns (bias/defaults, privacy, disclosure/attribution, dependence) plus speed, name every concern that's genuinely in play — not just the one that occurred to you first. Be honest about which ones actually conflict here, and which don't apply at all.
stages.checkpoint: You have a one-sentence decision statement and a real list of which of the phase's concerns are actually at stake, not a padded list including ones that don't apply.

stages.title: Apply the framework and reach a call
stages.instructions: For the concerns that conflict, apply the irreversibility-first heuristic from lesson two: which harm, if it happens, can't be undone? Use lesson three and four's stakes-and-claim reasoning to check your instinct against the actual factors, not just your gut. Reach an actual call — not 'it depends,' a specific decision you're making.
stages.checkpoint: You have a specific, stated call, with the irreversibility and stakes reasoning that produced it written out, not just asserted.

stages.title: Write the memo and the rule it produces
stages.instructions: Write the actual memo: the decision, the reasoning (concerns identified, irreversibility check, stakes/claim analysis), and the call. Then extract the general rule this decision teaches you, and write where you'll actually place it using lesson five's placement principle — not just 'I'll remember this.'
stages.checkpoint: The memo is complete and specific, and the extracted rule has a real, named place it will live going forward.

rubric.criterion: The decision is real, not hypothetical
rubric.meets: This is an actual decision from your own work or life, genuinely ambiguous to you when you started.

rubric.criterion: The concerns identified are honest, not padded
rubric.meets: Only concerns genuinely in play are listed — the memo doesn't force-fit all four just to look thorough.

rubric.criterion: The irreversibility reasoning is explicit
rubric.meets: States specifically which harm was treated as irreversible and why, not just 'I weighed everything.'

rubric.criterion: The call is a real decision, not a hedge
rubric.meets: States an actual, specific call — not 'it depends' or 'more information is needed' as a final answer.

rubric.criterion: It would survive a real skeptic
rubric.meets: Reading it as someone who disagreed with the call, the reasoning addresses the strongest objection, not just the easy one.

rubric.criterion: The extracted rule has a real, named placement
rubric.meets: States specifically where the resulting rule will live going forward, per lesson five's placement test — not just 'I'll remember this.'

contentSections.body: This is the actual point of the whole phase: not memorizing five modules of scenarios, but being able to run the reasoning, honestly, on one decision that's genuinely yours.
